And then the fact that it can be harnessed in this agentic fashion to do things that are not within human experience, but just bootstrapped on it, is its own flavor of wild.
And for all the flavors of wild and weirdness that you can see visible in the physical universe right now, reflected in the S-1, et cetera, et cetera, we haven't seen anything yet. I think that might be a good thing to say. We mutually expect to be more surprised in the future than we have been surprised in the last five years of being surprised, right?
That is the correct way to be calibrated.
Capabilities versus diffusion
Zvi: Absolutely. I think so far, I would summarize it as: I have been surprised the models have gained capability as quickly as they have so far. And, like everybody else, I have been surprised, conditional on how much capability they have gained, at how little the world around us looks different as a result of that.
Diffusion has been slower than I would have expected, but ultimately that doesn't matter. And as the models themselves are capable of driving the diffusion, the diffusion will speed up. So yes, expect high weirdness.
Patrick: I think I was far worse calibrated than yourself and other people on the rate of advances in capabilities, and better calibrated with respect to diffusion.
They are diffusing faster than my model for diffusion. (“Diffusion” here is the term of art, folks, for how fast capitalism is adopting these things.)
[Patrick notes: My naive model for diffusion was “It takes capitalism about 10-15 years to get this into All The Things beginning at GPT 3 levels of capabilities.” You’re welcome to compare that to e.g. AI 2027. Importantly, I think one thing I believe which is not widely believed was that GPT 3/3.5 was already sufficient to kick off an industrial revolution, given sufficient effort to harness it.]
Zvi: Yeah, I don't think I was crazy stupid high on rate of diffusion, but I do think I was substantively high on that. And it seems so crazy to me. You look around and you're like, "Well, they have these fantastic things that can do all these cool things for you for very cheap.
Why are people not investing in it?" And people don't do things. It takes a while. They need to see other people do them. They need to have it kind of just naturally there, step by step, without having to make any leaps or make any investments.
Patrick: Yeah. And to be clear, when we are saying that capitalism is not doing anything with these yet, it's like there's only tens of billions of dollars a year spent on inference.
I mean, clearly, if we were serious about things, we'd already be at trillions.
And nothing is investment advice, et cetera, et cetera, et cetera. But you'd have to assume crazy things about the world to assume that we don't get to trillions of dollars in spend on inference: either a complete collapse of inference costs, or, I suppose, the death of all humans, or massive contraction in the world economy, et cetera, et cetera.
These things provide cognition on tap. There is not an obvious ceiling for how valuable that is.
Zvi: Yeah, I mean, obviously it's possible that five years from now, it will turn out that model capabilities de facto kind of peter out for most practical purposes, and the model everyone uses costs a tenth or a hundredth of what we currently pay for our frontier models, and it's just very, very compute efficient. And then we'll just use that much more of it, right?
In that situation, because it'll be so good and so valuable, and we'll have had time to figure out what to do with it.
Token spend at the frontier
Patrick: Do you have any anecdotes for — if you think of the people in your social/professional set and similar — what the peak is for token usage per month at the moment?
Zvi: So I'm in a weird spot where I'm a writer, so I don't really code massive things, and I don't hit limits, right? I have the max subscriptions, because it's very important to me to never hit a barrier, and also it's very important for me to be able to have access to everything on the first day, so that I can evaluate it and report back.
Even if most people can wait a week and it doesn't really matter.
Patrick: I am not at liberty to say who it is yet, but I can say I'm aware of at least one person who spends more than a million dollars a month in inference for the acceleration of their professional job, and whose employers look at their inference spend every month and are like, "Great.
That continues to grow. Wonderful." And there don't have to be all that many people in the world hitting a million dollars a month in spend that they can personally authorize for these to be wild, wild businesses. And again, the job of this person in the status quo resembles the job that they were doing two years ago, except they're now doing just a whole lot more of it, because they have teams of minions. Virtual minions.
Zvi: Yeah. My guess is that the fact that I'm not spending at least ten times as much as I am on inference, and probably a hundred times, is mostly a skill issue. I have chosen not to prioritize figuring out how to do that. But it just seems absurdly like I should be doing that.
Patrick: Yep.
I feel just the same way. I'm sometimes thinking of hiring for this podcast, and if I was being strictly rational about it, it would just be spending four weeks on "automate all the things." But I have not done that yet, even though I make extensive use of AI in various parts of the production function here.
Final thoughts on the S-1
Patrick: So do you have any more thoughts on the Anthropic S-1 that we have not already covered?
Zvi: So I think those are the main ones. It's just sort of — they chose mostly a standard corporate document to write, and they are presenting as if they might have very, very fast growth, and they gave us very, very attractive, very good financials and prospects.
But aside from the corporate structuring that we got more detail on, and the choice of how they communicated, I felt like, sort of — it wasn't like the central issues were news, right? We knew vaguely where Anthropic was at. They'd already shared a bunch of details in advance. And so we're all looking at it to sort of get a slightly better feel, get a bunch of details that we didn't have.
But yeah, I think that Anthropic's S-1 was the S-1 we always knew was coming, to a large extent. I would've been very surprised — very pleasantly — if they had stepped up to the plate and issued a much more robust warning, but I wasn't expecting it.
Patrick: The one micro note I would have that we haven't already discussed is, the S-1 at one point explicitly contemplates capabilities growth and product improvement, and Anthropic creating products which economically dwarf their products to date.
And we've indeed seen a couple of iterations of this, where they had the API, and then they had the chatbot on top of the API, and then they have Claude Code, which is something much different than a single-threaded chatbot, and are continuing to build on from there. I've always perceived the chatbots for the labs as being essentially a sales engineer for the real product, which is the API.
But the agents and harnesses seem to be, quote-unquote, "the correct way" to use the API, versus single-threaded calls. And we will see if that is still true two years from now. But they are certainly where the economic interest is at the moment. And it is possible that, as they get tighter and tighter into this self-improvement loop, there are more tiers of the business that don't cause the previous business to go to zero, but they cause it to be economically irrelevant, because they're just worth so much more.
Which is a wild thing to say, when the thing that will be economically irrelevant is the one that was doing 15x revenue gain on a base of more than a billion dollars. But we are priced into a wild, wild few years, regardless of what happens to stock prices or individual returns to securities, I think.
The hackening and who bears responsibility
Zvi: Yeah, I mean, I think that's pretty much guaranteed, and the pace of things is accelerating. The Hackening is only getting worse, it looks like, over the last few days, so.
Patrick: Can we discuss that briefly? I think there's going to be a bit of backlash against the labs for this, because — I don't think it's true that the labs made us more vulnerable to it.
Software has been insecure for the entire lifetime of software. That's the default way to create it. We are lately getting exposed to the bill via AI-uplifted hack incidents, where, in most cases, it seems like the actual tool used to uplift the hackers was not directly one of the labs' products, but it was one of the open-weights models that were created with substantial reliance on distilling the labs' products.
(Although there have been cases of documented misuse of the labs' products directly against various targets.)
And so yesterday we had two major incidents, where I started the morning thinking, "Wow, Polymarket had a loss which was large and inconsequential." And then Binance had a hack loss north of $5 billion and counting, to North Korea. Which, speaking of AI impacts on the global economy — we have already passed the point at which AI is more than 5% of the GDP of a nation.
It's more than 5% of the GDP of North Korea, by enabling them to innovate in their business model of stealing money from crypto people. And I shouldn't kick crypto too much. They're only stealing the money from crypto people preferentially because that is the lowest-hanging fruit. After they have taken many more billions of dollars from the crypto industry, they will start hitting the rest of us more aggressively than they currently do.
But I think people are going to get to a period where, wow, it is now obvious that we need — my estimate is like $500 billion of remediation, at least at pre-LLM prices. And this $500 billion feels, to some, like a ransom demand from the labs, because the only way we can reasonably pay it is by adopting AI for the blue team, for defenders, et cetera, et cetera.
And "you created the problem, and now you're selling us the solution to it for tens of billions of dollars" is going to discomfit some people. What are your thoughts on this?
Zvi: So I feel like you're painting kind of the optimistic case, where there's this fixed set of technical debt that we incurred, and mostly it's just the bill is coming due much faster than it would've otherwise come due, which is forcing you to deal with this via AI, which is going to cost you a lot of money, but is ultimately a one-time bill that you can pay, and then the problem is solved.
I don't think of it that way.
Patrick: I also don't think of it as a one-time bill, but just the backlog is already priced into $500 billion.
Zvi: Right. The issue is that the moment we get down that $500 billion, I don't think that that results in something that is now robust. I think that's like, now the next level of things, the next set of dominoes, start to fall.
I think it was very reasonable, obviously, to build the entire internet and the entire modern world around things that were not fully secure, because being fully secure is next to impossible. And previously, there was a very fixed pool of people who were, one, trying to cause trouble; two, had capacity and knowledge to cause trouble; and then three, targeting you and your thing specifically, because there are so many things in the world and not that many people left to target them.
And now you can probe and exploit at scale, in parallel, and any number of people can do it, and those capabilities are going up, and they can concentrate their firepower on whatever they decide the weak spot might be at any time, including figuring out where the weak spot might be in order to concentrate their firepower.
Yeah, it's going to be dramatically, dramatically harder. And I am not one of those who has the maximalist view of "the internet will break," or you will assume that any phone that activates its Wi-Fi will immediately get rooted. I don't think these are likely scenarios, but I do think that we're going to lose a lot of the internet, probably permanently, on the long tail.
A lot of things are going to go down reasonably often. A lot of things are going to get stolen. A lot of things are going to get compromised. A lot of information's going to leak. We're going to have a continuous set of problems. Will the labs be blamed for this? I mean, somewhat, sure, but they should be blamed for this, right?
There would not be these Chinese models that are capable of doing this without the American models.
Patrick: Huh. I think there's complicated notions of desert there, where I agree that but for the labs having state-of-the-art models, this state would not be occurring. I don't know whether it is reasonable to lay at their door consequences of decisions made by other people using their technology. I similarly don’t know whether it is reasonable to argue they simply didn't get distillation locked down quickly enough, and now they are in some way morally responsible for the consequences of that.
Zvi: I mean, I think that's a good point to close on: it's just sort of, it's not the incentives, it's you. And this goes to existential risk, and potentially building things that will lead to an AI race that gets everybody killed when we don't know how to control things that are smarter and more capable than ourselves, or when this creates equilibria that have no good solutions that we know of, and where all the natural outcomes are extremely bad.
And it also applies to hacks, where any individual decision makes sense, but inevitably goes down this road, and you didn't actually figure out how to mitigate this sufficiently. You didn't actually figure out how to fix it. And they've done some very commendable things, like Glasswing and Daybreak and so on, to try and mitigate the situation.
I'm sure it'd be vastly worse if they hadn't done those things. But at the end of the day, yeah, it's not the incentives, it's you. Don't pretend that just because someone else would've done it, that gives you the okay to do it, because then someone else is pointing at you.
Trapdoors and irreversible decisions
Patrick: I will say that there is an element of trapdoor-ness to — we are making decisions that are not fully reversible.
And that has been obvious for a few years, but there were, I think, many people involved who had reasonable points of view in a world where you think you would be able to have take-backs. And so there's many people in the tech industry, including many people who have dumped a lot of money into lobbying on this issue, who are quite committed to open source models being available as a thing.
And once the open source models and the open weights achieve a capability, that is the worst capabilities will ever be going forward, unless you successfully do a worldwide surveillance regime over all basic computing, which is hopefully impossible. It would be an incredibly dystopian world if we were able to blacklist mathematics.
So once it's out there, it's out there, and it is now out there with the capability of uplifting North Korea and other bad actors. And we will never be able to yank that back. We can only go forward from where we are right now. And I hope we learn the lesson of that with respect to things like — by the standards of things that AI could potentially do, stealing $5 billion from Binance is a prosaic risk.
There will be other trapdoors in the future, and we do not want to fall down those trapdoors as well. And I guess that is as good a place as any to call it. Well, Zvi, thanks very much for discussing. These days, your newsletter continues to be kind of essential for people trying to keep up on the frontier here.
Where can people find that?
Zvi: You can find my newsletter at thezvi.substack.com.
Patrick: Thanks very much for being on the program. And to everybody else out there, thanks very much for listening, and we'll see you next week on Complex Systems.

articles.title: Inkling 2 Small
articles.body:
Today we are introducing our second model generation with Inkling 2 Small. It is a Mixture-of-Experts model with 594B total parameters, 17B active, and supports image inputs and variable effort.
Inkling 2 Small far surpasses our previous models’ scores on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index with a score of 31, reflecting gains in performance on agentic coding, vision, knowledge work, and reasoning. The increase in capabilities comes from improvements made at every step of our training process, including more efficient pre-training and a large, unified RL run.
Inkling 2 Small will initially be available through Tinker, with closed weights, following the approach we outlined in a safe path to open weights. We intend to make the full weights available under an Apache 2.0 license next week after the completion of external safety testing and red-teaming.
You can try Inkling 2 Small on Tinker Playground today. The model is also available for fine-tuning and sampling on Tinker; checkpoints will be downloadable with the release of Inkling 2 Small’s weights.
Capabilities
Inkling 2 Small is more capable across the board than our first generation, particularly in long-horizon autonomous work.
Inkling 2 Small’s vision and agentic capabilities enable it to incorporate visual feedback to iteratively build and refine websites, games, and 3D designs with interactive elements.
Agentic coding and autoresearch
Inkling 2 Small was trained with RL on hundreds of thousands of long-horizon coding tasks across multiple agent harnesses and context-compaction strategies. We increased the quality of our synthetic coding data pipeline and moved beyond unit-test rewards alone; many tasks included an agentic RL grader that evaluated how the model approached the problem, not just whether its code passed. We also tested early checkpoints of Inkling 2 Small on OpenCode under the name Fledge-Alpha to assess our model’s performance on coding tasks in the real world.
The result is a model that is both stronger at coding and easier to use inside real agent loops. Inkling 2 Small improves on usability compared to Inkling: it follows instructions better, considers changes carefully, and verifies its work without being asked.
Beyond conventional software tasks, Inkling 2 Small was also trained on long-horizon autoresearch tasks. This included agentic GPU kernel optimization and ML tasks such as post-training a model autonomously, all run across a range of GPU architectures.
To demonstrate its end-to-end autoresearch performance, we tested Inkling 2 Small on a task Proximal built for one of our internal benchmarks. Inkling 2 Small autonomously trained Qwen3.5-4B on Tinker to predict various time series such as weather and Wikipedia page views. It started by analyzing the tasks and writing its own evaluator, experimented with training datasets and recipes, and tried various approaches to SFT and RL, while debugging the process as it goes. After 4.5 hours of work and $426 in Tinker spend, the trained model has more than doubled its forecasting score.
Vision interpretation and creation
Inkling 2 Small processes image inputs using a 292M-parameter vision encoder based on Perception EncoderBolya et al., 2025.. We use 20×20-pixel patches with 2×2 spatial pooling, and interleave image patches with text tokens. The model demonstrates strong visual capabilities across multiple categories, including OCR, grounding, infographic interpretation, and visual reasoning.
The model uses vision in the loop to interpret and validate the visual coding output it generates. Pending the release of its weights, it is set to be the top open-weights model on DesignArena.
We even tested Inkling 2 Small against some of our researchers in a wine tasting event. It outperformed them using vision alone, correctly identifying three wines from a single picture in 19 out of 20 trials.
Agentic knowledge work
Inkling 2 Small accelerates knowledge work in realistic professional environments. It proficiently looks up information, calls tools over MCP, and produces high-quality deliverables. On AA-Briefcase, an end-to-end knowledge work benchmark, these capabilities come together for an ELO score of 1527.
Inkling 2 Small is especially strong in finance and quantitative reasoning over spreadsheets, filings and documents. Among open weight models, Inkling 2 Small is the best performing model across several finance benchmarks.
Customizability
Some models respond better to fine-tuning, independent of their out-of-the-box performance. We wanted Inkling 2 Small to be a strong base model for customization.
Inkling 2 Small learns faster and improves more than our previous models when trained on the same data and algorithm across a variety of post-training scenarios, which we curated based on customer use cases. For example, starting from similarly low scores on a public financial-document summarization task, Inkling 2 Small adapts quickly, reaching the final performance of Inkling Small with just 75 training steps and finishing substantially ahead.
Reasoning, knowledge, and epistemics
Inkling 2 Small is trained on challenging STEM problems, instruction following, information seeking with and without web search, and forecasting tasks. During RL, we use proper scoring rules for forecasting tasks and uncertainty-sensitive rewards on some question-answering tasks. This trained the model to assess uncertainty, express appropriate confidence, and make well-calibrated predictions.
Safety and alignment
Our safety work for Inkling 2 Small centers on two questions: how the model performs for the general user, and how well it resists the removal of safeguards by a malicious actor. The release of Inkling’s weights is pending further safety evaluations by us and our partners.
To assess misuse risks, we trained an internal helpful-only variant. We ran both this model and the release checkpoint through a wider suite of evaluations, with more external testers, than any previous release.
On chemical, biological, radiological, and nuclear (CBRN) risk, Inkling 2 Small’s knowledge and capability scores sit below the open-weight frontier. On FORTRESS, Scale AI’s private benchmark that scores how much harmful assistance a model gives in response to expert-written adversarial prompts across CBRN, terrorism, and nonviolent crime, Inkling 2 Small has a lower Average Risk Score compared with Inkling and Inkling-Small, and also demonstrates a higher Overrefusal Score (see Limitations). The helpful-only variant of Inkling 2 Small exhibits marginal uplift on CBRN knowledge relative to the release checkpoint, but it does not significantly advance the frontier on any dimension we measured.
On offensive and dual-use agentic cyber benchmarks, Inkling 2 Small is a large step up from Inkling Small but remains behind the open-weight frontier. It matches the open-weight frontier on Vals CyberBench v1.1 and PatchEval, both of which measure the ability to find and patch security vulnerabilities.
* While we handle mental distress situations well, our model sometimes overreacts with disclaimers in normal emotional support queries as mentioned in the Limitations section.
As models take on unsupervised, longer-horizon autonomous work, the potential harm from their misbehavior increases. Without proper attention to alignment, capabilities-focused RL can push models to succeed at any cost. When tasks were difficult, early checkpoints of Inkling 2 Small were persistent in trying to succeed—in some cases fabricating results, ignoring instructions, and concealing what they had done.
We worked across the stack to improve model alignment. In midtraining, we filtered out traces containing misbehavior and included traces with honest, aligned behavior. In RL, we added a general alignment reward that penalizes misbehavior on every task. We also built environments targeting specific failure modes we observed in training, such as rewarding models for giving up on impossible tasks. Finally, we used on-policy self-distillationZhao et al., 2026; Shenfeld et al., 2026. from a teacher model prompted with a conduct spec, so the model internalizes principles for good behavior without explicit prompting.
We measured progress with both internal and external evaluations, and found that Inkling 2 Small substantially improves over previous Inkling models on both internal and external evaluations, and outperforms a set of comparable open-weights models on our internal evals.
Inkling 2 Small still trails closed-weights models, such as GPT-6.1 Sol on our alignment evaluations. Reducing this gap is a priority for future models.
We also worked to secure training and evaluations with two layers of monitoring. The first is synchronous: a monitor inspects tool calls before they run. Each task declares what actions it authorizes. Deterministic rules check calls against the task’s policy and circumvention patterns, escalating uncertain cases to an LLM judge. The second layer is asynchronous: an LLM judge reviews completed rollouts from training and evaluation for misbehavior and actions against our security boundary, raising alerts that we triage and escalate into our incident process. Together, these form a defense-in-depth approach to safety and alignment that we consider critical to developing a safe model factory.
Training Inkling 2 Small
Inkling 2 Small’s initial pretraining phase (H1) covered 8.4 trillion tokens of a broad mix of natural language, code, and image data. It ran for 68 hours on NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 racks, which enabled high expert parallelism. Training ran natively in NVFP4, the 4-bit floating-point format introduced with the NVIDIA Blackwell GPU architecture. We’ll share more details on our NVFP4 recipe in a follow-up post soon.
We followed this initial phase with a second phase (H2) of 3.8 trillion tokens of higher-quality, newer data the model hadn’t seen, at 512K context. The third and fourth phases mixed in data in the deployment format. The third phase was about 320 billion tokens of reasoning and agent trajectories at 1M context, alongside replayed pretraining data. The fourth phase (H4) kept only the highest-quality data: about 34 billion tokens of agent trajectories. The H3 and H4 mixtures consisted mostly of trajectories sampled from earlier models including Kimi K3 and our own models, filtered for correctness and alignment.
We then carried out a joint RL run, consisting of 1,075 steps and over 17 million rollouts over 9 days. See table below for more details. This single joint run contrasts with the previous Inkling release, where we ran separate reasoning and agentic RL runs and combined them with multi-teacher distillation.
The task mix included software engineering in real repositories, terminal tasks, document creation, STEM question answering, vision, web app building, tool use with simulated users, and safety. Each task family had its own grader:
hidden unit tests and programmatic checks for most coding work;
rubric-based LLM judges for documents and tool use;
reference answers for STEM and vision question answering;
pairwise reward models comparing screenshots of rendered web apps.
We randomly sampled and conditioned on an effort level, and applied a length penalty in the reward function, which trained the model to trade off speed and thoroughness.
Our asynchronous RL uses a score centering variant—the StableReinforce objective in Tinker—which tolerates significant staleness. Our run combines short and long horizon tasks with p50/p99 total rollout tokens being 43k and 1.5M respectively and p50/p99 duration of 8 minutes and 4 hours respectively. We use 256k context length and enable compaction training for long-horizon tasks. As a result, both training reward and evaluation performance grow log-linearly with compute.
Making this scale practical required improvements throughout the systems stack. Our RL infrastructure deploys NVFP4 MoE training and sampling. During sampling, prefill, draft, and verify run fully on CUDA graphs. Trainers mirror the pretrain stack with high expert parallelism, EPLB, and CUDA graphs to improve GPU efficiency. To support long horizon agentic workloads, we use sticky routing and DRAM KV-cache offloading for maintaining 93%+ prefix cache hit rate, allowing us to maintain a 5:3 sampler:trainer ratio despite training at long contexts. Weight transfer is done via GPUDirectRDMA at 93%+ line rate with a parallelism-invariant checksum verifier. We also further lower deployment inference cost by offering a variant of NVFP4 KV cache, which we find to minimally lower evals.
Long-horizon tasks give the model hours of autonomy, increasing potential risks from misaligned behavior. Midway through the main RL run, our asynchronous monitor flagged an instance where the model, failing at a task, worked around a network block through a third-party service it could reach using its search tools. We paused the run, hardened our infrastructure, removed environments that required web access, and added synchronous tool-call monitoring. We then resumed the run, incorporating additional training phases specifically for alignment, as described above.
Improvements to our process allow us to train models at different sizes using similar recipes with predictable scaling and performance. Inkling 2 Small is part of a ladder of models; we look forward to sharing more rungs with you soon.
Benchmarking Inkling 2 Small
Like previous Inkling releases, we benchmarked Inkling-Small on a broad range of capabilities. All evals run at effort 0.99 (xhigh) and temperature 1.0. All evals run with a 1M-token maximum trajectory limit, increased from the 256K-token limit used for Inkling Small.
Highest reported score in each row; ties includedSecond-highest reported score in each row; ties included
Evaluation snapshot: Missing results are shown as dashes.
Limitations
While Inkling 2 Small improves on usability vs Inkling, it is not the most succinct communicator, and doesn’t always choose the best tools for the job—especially in codebases with a large number of skills.
Like previous Inkling models, Inkling 2 Small natively supports image input; however, this model does not support audio.
Inkling 2 Small is also less optimized for the chat experience. We notice issues such as worse organization and presentation of content, overuses of slashes, and overreaction to mental health and other safety related queries.
Try Inkling 2 Small today
We are proud to make Inkling 2 Small available on Tinker for inference and fine tuning. Following the completion of safety testing, the model will be available on additional platforms in the coming weeks.
Inkling 2 Small was made in service of our mission to build AI that extends human will and judgment. We hope that it encourages your ambitions, and we look forward to seeing what you build with it.
