articles.title: Nvidia Kubernetes Engine (NVKE)
articles.body:
Run a managed Kubernetes service on your own NVIDIA GPU infrastructure.
NVIDIA Kubernetes® Engine (NVKE) provides the management plane that platform teams install to create and
operate Kubernetes clusters for their customers. Each workload cluster has its
own Kubernetes control plane, etcd and node pools. You operate the NVKE management
plane; your customers use their clusters through the Kubernetes API and kubectl.
Preview: NVKE is available as a preview. APIs, configuration and behavior can change between releases, and we do not recommend NVKE for production workloads. See Preview status and known limitations.
Get started · Documentation · Contribute · Get help
The local quickstart runs on a Linux host or VM, amd64 or arm64, with at least
6 CPUs, 12 GiB of free memory and 100 GiB of free disk. It requires Docker,
virtual TPM support and the tools listed in the guide. Follow its setup through
workload-cluster creation and confirm the cluster's nodes report Ready.
On macOS, use the local site guide, which runs
the evaluation inside a Colima virtual machine.
For a real installation, you supply the machines, networking, node images and registries, and configure access to NVIDIA Infra Controller (NICo). NICo is the sole compatible infrastructure provider at preview. The platform and version reference lists validated combinations and pinned dependencies.
- Creates independent workload clusters. Request clusters through the NVKE
API or nvkectl; NVKE provisions machines through NICo and forms Kubernetes
clusters with their own control planes.
- Manages workload cluster lifecycle. Create, scale and delete node pools, upgrade Kubernetes and replace nodes. See the node pool guide for the manual steps and preview limits on replacement and upgrades.
- Establishes node identity. Nodes attest through SPIFFE/SPIRE using their TPM before receiving join credentials. Encryption of etcd data is available per cluster.
- Connects builds to deployment. Its companion project, NVIDIA Kubernetes Recipes (NVKR), builds node images and NVKE components from pinned inputs. NVKE deploys those artifacts; NVKR owns their build and release evidence.
The preview needs explicit operator configuration: API authentication is off and the API uses plain HTTP after installation. articles.title: Lippitt-Knoster in Practice (Field Notes for Managing Complex Projects)
articles.body:
"Lippitt-Knoster" is one of those things where if you've worked with me during the last 10 years, you've likely heard me mention it. You might even be reading this because I needed somewhere to point you. In which case, Hi! 👋
The Lippitt-Knoster Model for Managing Complex Change was originally written to describe a way of navigating large organizational shifts, but I’ve found that it’s also useful as a diagnosis tool for any kind of large and long-running project. After all, every project is a "change" in a microcosm. You might not have a complex organizational change to manage every day, but everyone is involved in long-running projects of some size and shape in a company. So that’s what I use it for, and it is useful indeed.
The beauty of the model is that you don’t need an MBA or a special issue of the Harvard Business Review to explain it. It says that any complex project requires six components to succeed, and if one or another is missing, you’ll have some specific and corresponding failure.
It can be summed up in a simple chart but also rewards you with some deeper insights as you apply it:
- Vision is the purpose and endpoint of a project. Vision tells you where you’re going and why. If the vision is missing, there will be confusion about what is being done and why work is happening.
- Consensus is a team's agreement and alignment around the vision. If a team lacks consensus, people will not want to do the thing and they will sabotage you.
- Incentives are the motivation or reasons for why people support the work and prioritize it appropriately. If not everyone is incentivized properly, there will be resistance. Resistance is the passive sibling of sabotage.
- The Action Plan is the practical set of steps to get from vision to finish. If you lack an action plan, your team will experience a routine set of false starts and treadmills, which is another way of saying that it will look like work is happening but nothing actually moves forward. You won’t make progress.
- Resources are the organizational capacity (people, budget, time) needed to accomplish the work. Lacking resources is a close cousin to lacking skills; it leads to frustration in trying to do something you know you're capable of, but with an unrealistic set of operating constraints.
- Skills are the ability to do the work necessary to complete the project. If a team lacks the necessary skills, you'll have a lot of questions around if this work is possible, leading to anxiety.
Vision, consensus, and incentives are all Strategic Concerns. They involve abstract political work: ideas, relationships, people, and an understanding of the business. The action plan, skills, and resources are all Tactical Concerns. They are focused on the practical details of “how” something gets done.1
One mistake I often see people make is to focus primarily on one concern or the other. For example, a product manager or corporate strategist might spend too much time focused on the strategic side of things without understanding if the team or company is able to execute. Consequently, their ability to build consensus will be negatively impacted by not knowing what is possible or probable. Line managers and software engineers typically make the opposite mistake. They focus too much on the ‘how’ instead of the ‘why’. They’ll prove that something is possible and how it can be done, without realizing that sometimes the team or business doesn't want to do the thing they’re proposing. Neither myopia ends in a successful project.
The order of the model components matters – they flow into each other – but can be managed in either direction. For example: you might start with a vision, build consensus, arrange the right incentives for everyone to act, create a plan, provide adequate resources and timeline to accomplish that plan, and make sure it is staffed with people who have the skills to execute on it. Easy peasy!
You could also navigate the components the other way, working through a series of questions: is something possible? Do skills exist to accomplish the thing? Do those skills (people) have excess capacity that can be allocated to this idea? Can it be done without budget? Can that group of people be small enough that they organically develop their own plans? And if so, are they incentivized to take on this kind of work outside their daily responsibilities? Does it need sign-off from anyone? If you’ve found confirmatory answers along the way, congratulations: you can carve out a secret R&D initiative within your team or your company. (This is also 'effectuation' in practice.)
You can also read the model from the perspectives of both cause and effect. Reading it one way creates a checklist before kicking off any major work: “Here are the six prerequisites for success, are we all set?” (A causal, prescriptive reading – given starting parameters, what will be the end result?) Reading it backwards turns it into a troubleshooting tool. For example, if someone comes to you mid-project complaining that "We keep going in circles and the team is anxious! What can I do?" you might look at the model and respond, "Well of course! You don't have an action plan. Or maybe, it hasn't been adequately distributed and communicated and people feel that they lack the skills to accomplish something so big. Let's break it down into manageable pieces that we do have the skills for." It’s pretty quick to go between looking at the failure states and looking at the necessary components to diagnose what’s going on with a project. (A diagnostic reading, reasoning backwards.)
The model is a fantastic tool for making sense of things. But that leaves the hard work to start after you've made sense of things. How do you drive consensus? How do you align folks around a vision? How do you build up skills, or break down big projects into smaller pieces for which skills exist? How do you win resources, or align incentives?
Some of those answers are obvious, but most are not. Many of the answers are best understood as the manifestation of tacit expertise — a ‘feeling’ for the right move in any particular context, a form of expertise that comes from having been around the block a few times.
And like with most tacit expertise, you’ll find that there are no one-size-fits-all answers to any scenario, but there are plenty of good practices and useful observations.
So here are some of mine:
Strategic Concerns
The most common and important questions that come up after someone lays out a vision are “Why should we do this?” and permutations around the follow-up details. If you see those questions, that’s “confusion”, which is another way of saying you’ve presented a fantasy instead of a vision (or perhaps, the vision is missing entirely). That’s because many people confuse vision for having a colorful and inspiring imagination, making their picture too colorful, unrealistically grand, or too far off.2
My experience is that you make more progress by simply providing adequate context and letting people derive their own vision. The art of context is giving people breadcrumbs to get from where you are today to where you want to be in the future, and giving them some good reasons to follow those breadcrumbs with you. There’s nothing more effective than a self-motivated team that thinks they’re the ones who came up with the idea, that they saw what things could be like. That’s vision.
Similarly, consensus is a straightforward concept, but strangely elusive in most organizations. Any organization beyond a certain age and size will typically have a 'minimally viable consensus' while practically being at odds with itself. Departments often turn into silos with their own internal logic for what should happen. Job security encourages teams to think about what’s best for them instead of for the company. And companies don’t do a great job tying “what’s best for the company” with “what’s best for the individuals within, or the communities around”,3 which makes most employment mercenary: people naturally find a balance between what they’re paid and how much to care about the thing in question. (In that sense, incorporated businesses are kind of like democracy: a bad choice, but among the best of the options available for coordinating large groups of people to accomplish things.)
Recognizing that, one amateur mistake people make is trying to build consensus in a group setting. It just doesn't happen that way. You’re either going to have everyone nodding along and afraid to say their piece in front of everyone else, or you’re going to have one guy (and it’s usually a guy – sorry, my dudes) start pulling some “what about”-ism and dragging the conversation into a black hole of details that you never intended to argue about but find yourself frustratingly debating anyway.
In either scenario, the meeting will end without consensus.
In Japanese business culture there is a concept called “nemawashi”, which translates roughly to “tending to the roots” or “laying the groundwork”. It’s a good analogy because the practice of creating consensus requires a lot of political skill, footwork, trust-building, and private conversation. It means giving people space to tell you everything that’s wrong with your idea, finding ways to address those concerns, and making sure everyone is aligned before the alignment actually happens. The group meeting when everyone signs off in agreement should be the result of careful stage management — you should know and have already addressed everyone’s concerns, including second-order effects of how addressing one person’s issues will impact others.
There should be no surprises; it is theater, not improv.
That said, you might not be able to get to consensus. Perhaps your boss wants the “thing” to happen but there’s another department that’s actively against it. Maybe you're encroaching on their turf, or it will reduce their capacity in some zero-sum resource bucket. Maybe they just have a different perspective on the world and the approaches the business should take. Maybe you've wandered into a long-running feud and this project is just one of many different battles being waged. Who knows, people can be both petty and complicated!
If you can't get their buy-in, they will sabotage it in all sorts of creative ways. Because sabotage and resistance are close cousins and are political (in the sense of not being open conflict), monographs on activism and subterfuge can be read as useful primers. Consider James C. Scott's Weapons of the Weak and the OSS's Simple Sabotage Field Manual for what kinds of foot dragging, malicious compliance, noncompliance, evasion, sowing confusion, slander, useless meetings, arbitrary hurdles, revisiting decisions, and moving goalposts to expect.
My advice for these scenarios is to try one of two things. Your first option is to get to the bottom of why there is no consensus and figure out if you’re in a position to address that root cause. Often, you’re not in a position to address those things; if you pursue resolution, you’re going to use up a lot of your political capital or burn out trying to get the project moving forward. And success can be fleeting – projects can continue to be sabotaged even after launch. I once had a project launch only to have all of its resources immediately pulled, forcing its premature death.
Not even chief executives are immune to this; sometimes the solution to a lack of consensus and active sabotage is to simply fire the people in disagreement. (Obviously, use this technique sparingly — you’re scorching the earth.)
So I recommend most people take the second approach, which is to just drop it. Move on. It’s a lost cause. Don’t be the sailor with a bucket trying to dump water off this Titanic. Quitting things and dropping things is a totally acceptable thing to do; life isn’t a video game where you’re striving for 100% completeness on every side quest. Move on to things where you’re actually making a difference.
But let’s say everyone agrees. Now you need to make sure that things are prioritized appropriately. You’re not going to make any progress if this is low on everyone’s priority list. So you incentivize teams and people.
Positive incentives typically work better than negative incentives, but most people are not in a position to offer meaningful (financial) incentives to push a project forward. Instead, you can rely on horse-trading (“if you help me move this project forward, I’ll help with your thing”), you can help people resolve their problems, and you can paint a compelling-enough end-state that people also want to reach that goal with you.
Otherwise, people are going to be resistant, which is a passive form of sabotage: sabotage without commitment, or general apathy. It might not even be malicious. It’s just… well, you’re just one more project for people to care about and work on. Why should they do it above all else?
And more importantly, resistance can turn into sabotage when incentives are not just missing, but misaligned. Misaligned incentives can break consensus when you're sweating the details.
Tactical Concerns
Now, let’s say you figured out the strategic bits and you’re working through the implementation portion. Some projects are simple enough that you can just describe what needs to be done, and you can count those requirements on a single maimed hand. We’re not talking about those projects.
Any complex-enough project requires coordination of requirements, dependencies, timelines, people, and other details. I’ve written a bit about those issues in “When Everything is Important But Nothing Is Getting Done”, so I don’t want to retread too much ground.
But one thing worth highlighting is how skills and anxiety are coupled, and how to navigate a lack of skills. Any ambitious project is at some point going to run into a lack of skills or prior experience because the work wouldn't be ambitious if you'd done it before. So in many regards, it is an existential question for any project: are you and your team able to do what needs to be done? If not, you’ll get a very stressed team, or you’ll get a simulacrum of what you expected.
There are ways to compensate for a lack of skills. I rely on three techniques:
First is up-skilling people. Education, mentorship, and training are effective ways to turn juniors into seniors, low-skilled employees into high-skilled employees. While there are a variety of documented techniques for this (see: accelerated expertise, tactical decision games), the caveats are that (a) this typically takes longer than the time-span of a single project and (b) you need to find people who are interested in learning.
So the second technique is atomization: break the requirements into smaller pieces that meet the level of skill available rather than trying to get people to rise to the required level. Instead of making everyone work harder, just make the requirements easier. Instead of asking people to “cut database reads by 50%” or “create a capacity forecasting model for the next 12 months” (where they may not even know where to start), give them smaller tasks and directions for what to do to accomplish that. Point folks in the right direction, explain the what and the why, turn big asks into a series of steps, a recipe to accomplish something. This is in itself a form of teaching, and it is more project-sized (see what I did there?).
The third technique is to roll up your sleeves and contribute. I’ve learned from many effective leaders that there is no work below your pay grade. What makes many great leaders "great" is their willingness to spend extra time doing “glue” work, filling in the holes between roles, and making sure all assumptions are bridged back to real expectations. They are never too good to personally write up a project document, to manage a tracker, to make sure that people are talking to each other. They often know as much or more about the details than subject matter experts, but they don't needlessly meddle – they support where needed and use gaps as up-skilling opportunities.
Much of the work of compensating for skills gaps is directly translatable into managing budget, time, and effort tradeoffs to navigate the “resources” component of Lippitt-Knoster. And your ability to solve for skills and resources directly translates back into the specific action plan you need to put together. For example: you may decide not to spend $100,000 on a vendor because you can reverse engineer a single feature you need for a project, but you need to add time to the plan for that.
These considerations become a calculus of risks, rewards, and effort, which in turn underpins the strategic portions that we talked about earlier: sure, you might think you can lead a team to rebuild the hot new vendor in house in two months, but have you earned organizational political capital to place those chips on the table?
So there you have it, Lippitt-Knoster in practice. Lead on!
1 - This grouping is not present in most Lippitt-Knoster model descriptions I’ve come across; it is my own humble contribution. The order I'm presenting it in is also my contribution – the order in Mary Lippit's original 1987 model is quite different, for reasons I couldn't discern.
2 - A realistic vision that is too far into the future is its own type of risk – every day presents new opportunities for conditions to change, starting conditions to be led astray. The likelihood of any far-off future has too many compounding variables... too many things have to go right and be true for it to be reliable enough to pin your hopes to.
3 - These things are usually at odds with each other. There's a big literature about how "equity" is a tool to get employees to care about corporate success, but most startup equity goes to zero; for the average employee, a bonus or a pay raise is more useful. Public company equity presents a different issue: it is dependent on public market behavior, and less on your individual ability to impact it – being in a public company, you're likely one of thousands-plus of employees.
Thanks for reading
Useful? Interesting? Have something to add? Shoot me a note at roman@sharedphysics.com. I love getting email and chatting with readers.
You can also sign up for irregular emails and RSS updates when I post something new.
Who am I?
I'm Roman Kudryashov -- I help healthcare companies solve challenging problems through software development and process design. My longer background is here and I keep track of some of my side projects here.
Stay true,
Roman

articles.title: Republicans Learn X Is the Echo Chamber
articles.body:
There's a BlazeTV YouTube video whose thumbnail shows the presenter with his arms around Anakin Skywalker and a gender-flipped Draco Malfoy called Malfoid. “Total Chud Victory?” It says. The video's title: “Young Right is Reclaiming Culture and Liberals Are Mad About it.”
BlazeTV posted the video on November 2, the day before Democrats swept the midterms and started a political realignment in America so overwhelming that Republicans lost control of all the most powerful state positions in Texas.
The video is a profound misreading of the political and cultural moment. It reminded me of stories of the Bolsheviks seizing the Winter Palace to discover tarot card playing courtiers who had no idea a revolution was happening in the streets.
The American version was watching defense contractor Palmer Lucky dress up like Harry Potter on Halloween while standing next to his Malfoid wife. And it was Elon Musk — who spent roughly half a billion on the election only to see his chosen candidates fail — posting an AI generated picture of Anakin Skywalker sitting at the head of a happy fascist Star Wars family two days before the midterms.
The online right has dominated American culture for a decade, or at least has dominated political narratives picked up by the mainstream media. Its memes and conspiracies drove news cycles. At first, the right’s memes filtered from random people on obscure Discord channels to Reddit’s r/the_donald or 4chan to Trump’s Twitter feed. More recently they’ve come from AI slop farms, from Musk, or from the administration itself. Powered by a well-funded media and podcast ecosystem, Fox News (and a propensity for shamelessness) its comedians, podcasters, and pundits became powerful celebrities and influencers, at least within Elon Musk’s X.
This insular, often inscrutable world has given us Ben Shapiro, Nick Fuentes, Gamergate influencers, the streamer Asmongold, and a revolving door of characters who have shuffled interchangeably between Twitterverse celebritydom and actual government; Kash Patel, DataRepublican, Laura Loomer, Pete Hegseth, RFK Jr., Dan Bongino, the list goes on.
It has been said many times that “Twitter is not real life,” and that posting too much anywhere will rot your brain. Never has that been more apparent than now: Much of Trumpworld spent the week before an election in which they would get utterly trounced using AI to generate barely legible Anakin and Malfoid memes for an inconsequential ingroup on the social media platform run by the biggest loser on the planet.
“It certainly seems like it has had its high water mark and that reality has FINALLY caught up with the Republican Party,” Michael Senters, a PhD candidate at Virginia Tech who studies online and gaming culture, told 404 Media.
In 2016, 4chan posters talked about “meme magic” — the pseudo-ironic belief that pictures on the internet could manifest great change in reality. According to legend, Trump strategist Steve Bannon was running a World of Warcraft gold farm when he realized the angry gamers could be harnessed into a powerful reactionary political force. Bannon and others would successfully parlay Gamergate into an endless culture war that’s dominated online life in the Trump era.
During the midterm livestream of Bannon’s War Room podcast, his guest read exit polls that suggested the right-wing had lost young men — a group long thought to be its strongest soldiers. The split between the parties was even, the guest explained. “That can’t be right,” Bannon whispered, signalling he’d lost touch with the constituency he’d harnessed on behalf of Trump ten years ago. As the election results began coming in, right-wing podcasters, livestreamers, and newscasters across the internet went through at least a few of the stages of grief. First they struggled to understand what was happening, suggesting the votes must be wrong. Eventually, many of them ragequit.
"Okay, I'm going to be honest. I'm absolutely rage quitting. I'm so frustrated. I am so unbelievably frustrated. I'm so mad. I think Trump didn't do 50 different things he should have done. I think he should have gone a thousand times harder. I think that he wasted his time selling trinkets and nonsense,” Asmongold said as the returns came in. He lives in Texas where Democrats swept in a shock victory.
“I wish that there were more people who thought like me that weren’t sorry about it. But you know what? There’s not. So it’s just me. And that’s fine. It’s fine. It’s OK,” he said, his voice catching in his throat.
Many right-wing personalities went into Tuesday somehow expecting to win despite a disastrous war, a disastrous economy, disastrous polls, and a doddering president whose closing argument seemed to be more about his ballrooms, golf courses, and the Reflecting Pool than anything else. Since Trump was re-elected, these same people have called everyone else out of touch, convinced by their X algorithm and prediction markets that no blue wave would materialize. The media has similarly spent many thousands of words suggesting that Bluesky is an out-of-touch leftist echo chamber while mostly failing to suggest anything of the sort about the AI-pilled Silicon Valley executives, bots, and racists shitposting on X. Tuesday’s election wipeout highlights how detached from reality the Malfoid/Anakin-shipping, X-brained billionaires and their acolytes have actually become.
“Blueskywave. Those of us on here, across the board, were out of touch. I see no other conclusion,” Joe Weisenthal of Bloomberg's Odd Lots podcast (who is a serious, good journalist), said in a post on X after the election amidst a sea of Anakins tonguing Malfoids.
The meme game and general demeanor of Trump and his followers has grown wildly tiresome in his thus far-disastrous second term. Under the guidance of White House Communications Director Steven Cheung, official government accounts have posted racist Halo memes, used AI to put a studio Ghibli face on anti-immigrant propaganda, and fully embraced Malfoid and Darth Vader as cultural heroes. The base on X loved this stuff. No one else did.
As our friend Gita Jackson over at Aftermath wisely put it immediately before the election, "The idea that they can meme magic their way into a red sweep by posting about Anakin Skywalker a lot is pure desperation [...] Their values have been rejected by popular culture at large, and they are now resigned to exist in the margins.”
Senters said the midterms showed the hard limits of memes as a political tool. “The power that memes have has always been, in my opinion, the power to help define linguistic and community lines in the amorphous space of the Internet. You create a community when you ‘get the joke’ behind a meme but memes generally don't persuade,” he said. “I'll be curious to see if the government accounts will continue to post these far-right cultural memes in the wake of the defeat or if they'll change their tune at all. Like do they double down on the meme posting to try to rally their base? Because it very clearly had ZERO appeal to anyone outside their base.”
Yet the right-wing has spent the last ten years acting as if their memes had moved the country politically. “They deluded themselves into believing that memes carry persuasive power and that their bubble on X represented material reality in a meaningful way when that was no way close to the truth,” he said. “They saw how many ‘numbers’ the Malfoid and Anakin memes did on X and convinced themselves that this was a real cultural awakening moment and that the volk were on their side.”
Alyssa Mercante, an internet culture reporter who is writing a book about politics and video games called Rage Game, agreed. “I think what it's really showing is that when you start to get a little bit too deep in the weeds of this hyper online culture war stuff, it cannot escape the internet,” Mercante told 404 Media. “It is not working anymore. The material reality of America is just not good enough.” Gas prices are up. Everything is more expensive. And ICE has killed Americans in the streets.
“This conspiratorial mindset is wrecker mentality. It is just destructive for the sake of destruction. You're just upending tables and pointing at them and laughing.”

In Nevada, Halo composer Martin O’Donnell ran as a Republican for a House seat and lost to incumbent Susie Lee. O’Donnell announced his campaign on Discord and leaned hard into an extremely online gamer identity. “He’s like, ‘I wrote the Halo music and I’m voting for Trump and you should too.’ He did a Halo LAN party campaign fundraiser. The imagery was him as Master Chief,” Mercante said. “This dude is like: ‘My personality is gamers, gamers are not woke and they're resisting this [...] and Trump is the person that is going to help us resist,’ and he's polling like absolute dog water.”
It’s been 12 years since Gamergate set the tempo for online culture wars and a decade since Trump won in 2016. In 2026, Star Wars, Halo, Harry Potter feel dated in a way they didn’t back then. “What 22-year-old kid is going to be like ‘they took Halo from me.’ They don’t know Halo to have it taken away from them,” Mercante said.
She stressed that so much right wing online culture is about distraction — she likened it to jingling keys to capture the attention of a baby. “If the economy is the number one issue for both Democrats and Republicans going into the midterms, no amount of Malfoid scissoring Anakin Skywalker is going to change that need for people to be in a better financial position,” Mercante said. “The tech oligarchs pushed this stuff straight into our eyes for two years straight unfettered [...] And I wake up and gas is this expensive? I don’t care if you take a Taylor Swift song and make JD Vance walk out to it.”
“[They] really thought that this would just last forever,” she added. “When you build up a meme presidency, eventually the cards just collapse underneath you, and there's just nothing to show for it.”
Though this midterm signals a move away from Gamergate-style culture war politics, both Senters and Mercante cautioned that this type of rhetoric is still dangerous, and can still be destructive. “They’re still very good at doing propaganda on the internet — they wrote the book in many cases,” Mercante said.

articles.title: Firecracker VM Escape: PwnEscape Part 2
articles.body:
Firecracker is supposed to keep untrusted code inside a microVM. We escaped it and achieved code execution as root on the host.
We found how it saved registers, changed where it would resume, and made it execute a call of our choosing when it returned from KVM. The guest then restored the temporary stack changes. Firecracker kept running, and the VM remained accessible over SSH.
PwnEscape Part 1 introduced the host memory primitive behind this work. Here we follow the next part of the chain: using that access to find Firecracker in memory and take over a live thread from inside the guest. This is a continuation to show CVE-2026-99999 on a Firecracker setup.
00 / Choosing where to take control
A Firecracker microVM has a process on the host that manages it. Each virtual CPU, or vCPU, has a thread in that process. The thread enters KVM to run the guest and returns to Firecracker when an event needs handling in userspace. Firecracker documents this arrangement in its architecture overview.
The call that runs the virtual CPU looks like this:
ioctl(vcpu_fd, KVM_RUN, 0);
While the thread is in that system call, the host kernel holds its saved userspace registers in a structure called pt_regs. These registers describe the Firecracker thread: its instruction pointer says where execution should resume, and its stack pointer says which userspace stack it should use.
That made the return from KVM_RUN an attractive target. If we could locate and modify the saved frame, we could choose the code Firecracker executed when the thread returned to userspace. A guest operation that caused such a return would provide the trigger.
We already had access to selected host physical memory through a guest mapping. To use it, we needed to identify the Firecracker process, find code we could call in that process, and locate the register frame belonging to its active vCPU thread. The starting point was a page of memory we controlled inside the guest.
Figure 1. The guest identifies its Firecracker process, finds the saved registers for a vCPU thread, and redirects the thread when it returns from KVM.
01 / Finding our guest page on the host
The guest and host use different physical address spaces. A page has a guest physical address, or GPA, inside the VM and a host physical address, or HPA, in the machine backing it. On the target, Extended Page Tables (EPT) provide the translation between them.
We placed a recognizable byte pattern, a nonce, in a guest page. The first resolver took that page's known GPA and its contents as inputs. Together, they gave us an address to translate and a way to check whether the translation reached our page.
The resolver searched the host physical ranges covered by the memory primitive for candidate EPT roots. An EPT root is the starting point of the translation tables. For each candidate, the resolver followed the entries selected by the guest address until it reached a physical page, then checked that page for the nonce.
The snippets below are explanatory pseudocode with descriptive helper names. They show the data passed between stages and the checks used to connect them.
for root in candidate_ept_roots:
page_hpa = walk_ept(root, guest_gpa)
if page_hpa is invalid:
continue
contents = read_host(page_hpa, length(nonce))
if contents == nonce:
candidates.append((root, page_hpa))
The nonce check connected a proposed translation to memory we controlled. The broader search produced two candidates; validation of the nested page tables reduced them to one EPT root. Walking that root gave us the host physical address of our guest page.
We called this result guest_page_hpa and passed it to the next resolver. We now had a recognizable object in host memory. The next task was finding the host process that mapped it.
02 / Finding the Firecracker process
Firecracker maps memory used by the guest into its own address space. That mapping gave us a way to work backward from the guest page to the process.
Host processes use page tables to translate their virtual addresses into physical memory. The top level is called the page global directory, or PGD. Recovering the appropriate PGD would let us translate addresses inside Firecracker and read its code and stack through the memory primitive.
Our reverse mapper searched the native host page tables for a mapping of guest_page_hpa. A normal page table walk starts with a virtual address and produces a physical address. Here, we looked for a mapping to a physical page we already knew, then recovered the virtual address and page table root associated with it.
The check runs in both directions:
for mapping in reverse_map_host_page_tables(guest_page_hpa):
pgd = mapping.root
guest_page_va = mapping.virtual_address
resolved_hpa = walk_host_page_tables(pgd, guest_page_va)
if resolved_hpa != guest_page_hpa:
continue
if read_host(resolved_hpa, length(nonce)) != nonce:
continue
process_candidates.append((pgd, guest_page_va))
This connected the host process's virtual mapping to the physical page found through EPT. The reverse mapper returned one validated address space. We retained its root as host_pgd and used it to inspect the process.
The next resolver looked for the Firecracker executable in those mappings. It identified an ELF image and checked a known byte sequence in Firecracker's write(2) wrapper. That connected the recovered address space to the binary we were targeting.
ASLR changes where an executable is loaded. The difference between an address in the ELF image and its corresponding runtime address is the load bias. Once the mapper had identified the image, it could recover that bias and use it to locate the code required by the exploit:
The mapper returned the load bias as firecracker_base. With that value and host_pgd, we could locate code in the running process, translate its virtual address to host physical memory, and compare the bytes there with the expected binary.
We checked three locations: the write(2) wrapper that would produce our proof, the continuation after the KVM ioctl, and a short xor eax,eax; ret sequence needed to return cleanly. Their purposes become relevant when we construct the return path below.
At this point, the guest could inspect the Firecracker image and its private mappings. We still needed the saved registers of the thread currently running our VM.
Figure 2. The nonce identifies the guest page in host memory. Its mapping leads to a host page table root, which lets the next resolver locate and validate the Firecracker image.
03 / Locating the live vCPU frame
The frame finder took host_pgd and firecracker_base from the preceding stages. It used them to recognize the host thread's saved state.
The most useful clue was the return address. A vCPU thread in KVM_RUN should have a saved instruction pointer at the corresponding ioctl continuation in Firecracker. We could calculate that address from the validated binary and its load bias.
We then searched host memory for a pt_regs frame consistent with that call. An address match alone would also pick up stale stack contents, so the candidate had to satisfy several related checks:
The stack check tied the frame to the same address space we had recovered from the guest page. The instruction and caller addresses tied it to the Firecracker image. The syscall fields tied it to the operation running the vCPU.
The search left one candidate. Its location was stored as frame_hpa, the host physical address of the saved register frame. We passed it, the PGD, and the load bias to the final helper.
Before changing memory, the helper repeated the code signature, frame, and stack checks. This ensured that the active stage used the same process state the resolvers had identified. The subsequent execution and recovery checks would establish that the selected frame was live.
Figure 3. The candidate register frame must agree with the KVM ioctl, the recovered process page tables, and the validated Firecracker code.
04 / Redirecting the return from KVM
We chose a simple payload: make the Firecracker process write a recognizable string to its own stderr. This would give the host runner an observable result from the process we had taken over.
The string was N8V23M2\n, seven characters followed by a newline. It occupies eight bytes and fits in one stack word. The call we wanted Firecracker to execute was:
write(2, "N8V23M2\n", 8);
Here 2 is Firecracker's stderr file descriptor. The buffer pointer must refer to the string in Firecracker's address space, so we stored the string on its private userspace stack.
We saved three stack words before modifying them. One held the string; the other two held the return addresses for the temporary call sequence. We then changed the saved register frame to supply the wrapper address, its arguments, and a stack pointer for that sequence:
RIP = address of Firecracker's write wrapper
RDI = 2
RSI = virtual address of the marker on Firecracker's stack
RDX = 8
RSP = virtual address of the temporary return sequence
Returning from write also needed care. A successful write of eight bytes returns 8, while a successful KVM_RUN call returns zero. We placed the address of xor eax,eax; ret first in the return sequence. It clears the return value before the second address brings execution back to Firecracker's original ioctl continuation.
The resulting control flow was:
KVM_RUN returns to userspace
-> Firecracker's write wrapper emits the marker
-> xor eax,eax; ret sets the return value to zero
-> execution resumes at the original ioctl continuation
With the stack and saved registers prepared, the guest wrote one byte to its serial port. That operation caused the vCPU thread to return from KVM_RUN. The kernel restored the modified registers, and Firecracker entered the write wrapper with our arguments.
The wrapper emitted the marker, the return sequence cleared eax, and the thread rejoined its original execution path. After control returned to the guest, the helper restored all three stack words.
Figure 4. The saved register frame enters the write wrapper. Two return addresses lead through the return-value adjustment and back into the original Firecracker path.
05 / Checking execution and recovery
The host runner captured Firecracker's stderr separately from the guest. The complete output was:
N8V23M2
The capture contained exactly eight bytes, including the final newline. Firecracker was still running, guest SSH was responsive, and the helper had restored the three temporary stack words.
We checked recovery with a fresh pass that made no memory changes. It was given the same frame address and repeated the register, code, and stack checks after the trigger. The checks passed, and it found no stale marker in the temporary stack location.
These observations answered three different questions. The guest log recorded the trigger and restoration. The host capture showed that Firecracker executed the selected operation. The final validation checked the state after execution.
Figure 5. The guest log, Firecracker stderr capture, and final validation record the trigger, host execution, and restored state.
06 / Root execution on the host
By the time the marker appeared, the guest had selected the host thread's instruction pointer, function arguments, stack data, and return path. Firecracker executed the call using its own privileges.
The target was Firecracker v1.16.1 on x86-64, with host kernel 7.0.0-1011-aws and guest kernel 6.18.44+. We launched Firecracker directly as root under systemd-run and pinned it with taskset. Consequently, the controlled call executed as root on the host.
The existing write wrapper gave us a compact proof of that control. Extending it to other calls would require choosing code and arguments compatible with the process's mappings and syscall policy.
The configuration used here had no jailer. Firecracker's production containment includes dropping privileges and restricting the process through namespaces and seccomp. A deployment using those controls requires a separate assessment of the privileges and resources available after compromising its VMM.
The address discovery is what lets the exploit follow the running instance. The EPT resolver connects a guest page to host memory; the reverse mapper recovers the host address space; the image mapper locates Firecracker under ASLR; and the frame finder identifies the vCPU's saved state. Adapting the final stage to another build requires validating that binary's code signatures and return path.
The guest had used access to host memory to take over the thread running the VM itself. A serial write supplied the trigger, and the next userspace operation belonged to us.
Captured resolver values and artifacts
The following values come from the preserved execution record. The methods above use symbolic names so that the role of each value is clear; this table connects those names to the recorded addresses.
The records use run ID eventpath-v23-0907self02 and boot ID 2b3cd5ac-2311-427f-a50a-6a79ecb8daa7. These identifiers connect the resolver records, host capture, and validation after restoration.
The earlier memory provider also received host-selected task and canary page frame numbers as independent validation overlays after constructing the memory aperture. Those addresses were not consumed by the EPT resolver, reverse mapper, Firecracker mapper, frame finder, or final marker helper.
The release bundle contains the final helper source, JSONL resolver records, host capture, recovery manifest, four preserved read-only resolver binaries with provenance, and SHA-256 manifests. The final helper accepts the PGD, load bias, and frame HPA produced by the resolvers. Its checks cover the run identifier, address ranges, code signatures, saved registers, and stack geometry; its dry-run mode performs validation without writing memory.
