articles.title: Promethevs: Full DeepSeek-v4.1-Flash-1017, locally, on 12GB of VRAM
articles.body:
The original model, not a smaller copy · 64 GB of RAM and one 12 GB NVIDIA card · free and open source
PROMETHEVS runs DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017, one of the strongest open models, from all 510 GB of its original weights, on an ordinary PC that cannot even load it: a Ryzen 9 3950X with 64 GB of DDR4, an RTX 3060 with 12 GB and two NVMe drives.
The PROMETHEVS engine gets there with compress-then-correct, a method devised by Ryan Flavell. Every word is first computed on a 2-bit copy of the model's experts. When the model itself is unsure (its top two choices are close), that word is recomputed with the original weights, rebuilt exactly from a stored correction plane. You get close to the speed of the compressed copy and close to the answers of the full model.
- Full-model quality, counted. On 960 audited words the output picks the full model's word 98.3% of the time (the 2-bit copy alone: 97.4%).
- Up to 7.4 tokens/s on a code prompt (warm cache, best case), against 2.14 for running the full model exactly on the same PC. Server runs: 5 to 8 on code, 4.5 to 5.4 on reasoning and agent prompts.
- Fast follow-ups. Only the first read of a long prompt is slow; the engine keeps what it has read, so the next message in a conversation starts in about 2 seconds.
- Works with your tools. An OpenAI-compatible endpoint on localhost, with streaming and tool calls, so apps and coding agents that speak the OpenAI API can use it.
- Private. The model runs on your PC; your chats stay there.
- Built from the original weights, on your machine. The installer downloads DeepSeek's weights and builds every store itself, checked against published hashes, so you do not have to trust our files.
- Free. Engine Apache-2.0; report, figures and logs CC BY 4.0.
New here? Check what you need, then install.
The hardware check in the bundle tests all of this and tells you up front if anything falls short. The full list is in engine-0.2/INSTALL.md.
- Download PROMETHEVS_0.2.zip from the latest release and extract it, for example to C:\promethevs_pkg.
- In PowerShell, from that folder:
powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File scripts\check_hardware.ps1        # checks the PC, picks the drives
powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File scripts\build_stores.ps1 --run    # downloads the weights, builds the stores (resumable)
powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File scripts\start_engine.ps1          # starts the engine (about 1 minute)
python scripts\py\verify_install.py --speed                                # checks it and measures the speed
- Point any OpenAI-compatible app at http://127.0.0.1:8100/v1, model deepseek-v4.1-flash-1017-promethevs, any non-empty API key. Close other programs that use the graphics card first.
Every step, the time and disk each one takes, and the known gaps are in engine-0.2/INSTALL.md. Release notes: engine-0.2/RELEASE_NOTES_0.2.md.
Measured on the build machine, 160 new tokens per prompt, two passes per run. Cold is a pass that starts with an empty expert cache. Warm is the second pass of the same prompt with the cache kept from the first, which is the best case for a cache; a real session that sends a different prompt lies between the two. Every individual run is in RESULTS.md.
Agreement is measured word by word against the word the exact path would choose given the same history. A slip is a difference the engine did not check, because the model was confident; the unchecked count counts those. Counting every difference also includes the words the engine checked and deliberately kept at a near-tie (both words almost equally likely). On its own the 2-bit copy picks the full-weight word on 97.4 percent of words; with the corrections, 98.33 percent counting every difference (99.17 percent by the unchecked count). The engine differs from the baseline build in two ways: it holds the draft head's experts in the 2-bit format too, and it keeps the expert cache from the first pass into the second. Keeping the cache lifted the code prompt but not the reasoning or agent prompts (the report gives the round timers behind this). In all three warm code passes no correction overturned a word, so the cache, the 2-bit draft head and the absence of an overturn are not separated, and 7.4 is a best case, not a typical session.
The PROMETHEVS engine does four things at once.
A 2-bit copy answers every word. The experts are stored in a 2-bit format that is smaller than the original FP4, so each word needs fewer bytes from disk. That is what makes the machine fast enough to be useful.
The model's own confidence picks the words to redo. For each word the engine looks at the gap between the model's top two candidates. When the gap falls below a threshold, the gate (0.45 here), the word is flagged.
Flagged words are corrected exactly. A stored correction plane turns an expert's 2-bit copy back into the exact FP4 expert, so a correction is the full model's answer for that word.
A draft head proposes several words at a time. DeepSeek ships a draft head with the model. The engine checks its guesses together in parallel lanes, which spreads the cost of reading experts across several words. The experts the model uses most sit in GPU memory; the rest live in RAM and on the two drives.
The method is compress-then-correct, devised by Ryan Flavell; the PROMETHEVS engine is built around it. Speculative decoding, quantised drafts and offloaded mixture-of-experts inference are the work it builds on; the report sets the method beside the closest references.
The build machine is a Windows 11 desktop with 64 GB DDR4, an RTX 3060 12 GB, and two NVMe drives (2 TB and 1 TB). The stores need about 1,009 GiB: 475 GiB of raw weights plus 534 GiB of derived stores (2-bit copies, correction planes, and FP4 copies of the first layers). Disk is the largest barrier for anyone repeating this. We kept each drive below about 90 percent full.
Every number above comes from one PC. If you run release 0.2 on your own machine, please send the output of python scripts\py\verify_install.py --speed and your engine log as a benchmark report. Reports are added here as they arrive.
Frontier-level AI today needs either a cloud subscription or hardware costing tens of thousands of pounds. Open-weight models are closing the gap with the closed frontier models, but running them still means someone else's server. PROMETHEVS, named after Prometheus, who in the myth brought fire to people, sets out to change that: frontier capability, at a speed close to the cloud, within 97 percent of what the original full weights would say, on a computer people already own. Release 0.1 published the method and every measurement; release 0.2 lets you run it.
Ryan Flavell. Compress-then-Correct Decoding: The Full DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 on a Five-Year-Old Gaming PC. PROMETHEVS Technical Report 1, version 0.1. MAGNVS Ltd, October 2026. doi:10.5281/zenodo.23577839
The report (PDF, Markdown) sets out the method, the measurements, where the time goes, what did not help and the related work. Every run behind it is listed in RESULTS.md, with the unedited logs in logs/.
- The technical report (PDF and Markdown) and its figures
- The logs behind every number in it, unedited (RESULTS.md lists them)
- The commands we ran to build the stores and the measurements (REPRO.md)
- Since 0.2: the engine server, its proxy, the hardware check, the store builder and the install check, as PROMETHEVS_0.2.zip on the v0.2 release (docs in engine-0.2/)
- A source rebuild that reproduces the shipped engine program byte for byte (0.2 ships it prebuilt, with its frozen build inputs; see gaps G1 and G2 in engine-0.2/INSTALL.md).
- A clean install of 0.2 on a second machine has not been run yet.
- Other platforms: 0.2 runs on Windows with one NVIDIA RTX 30 or 40 series card, and serves one request at a time.
- A reproduction on a second machine, and a demo of a real agent session.
We measured agreement against our own exact path; we have not yet run DeepSeek's reference implementation side by side. Speeds vary by prompt and by run, so we give every run. No prompt reaches the 8 tokens/s milestone we set, and the reasoning and agent prompts run below 5.3. First-word time on long prompts is read-bound: on a 1,163-token prompt the first word arrives after about 126 s (98 s with a candidate prompt-reading setting whose effect on quality we have not fully measured). The 99.17 percent figure covers three prompts of 30, 76 and 1,163 tokens. On a further 1,101-token agent prompt the engine scores 97.80 percent and the baseline build 97.16 (9 slips in 317 words), 0.16 points above our 97 percent contract at the gate we use (at gate 0.30 it falls to 96.21 percent); on a 4,288-token prompt the engine scores 100 percent and the baseline build 99.69. Counting every difference, both builds fall below 97 percent on the 1,101-token prompt (95.91 and 95.58 percent). Each long-prompt audit is one run. The chat template matches DeepSeek's encoder on six plain conversations; tool results and thinking mode are unchecked. All numbers come from one machine, one model and one prompt family.
REPRO.md outlines the steps we ran: download and verify the weights, build the stores, set the profile, run the benchmark. The scripts themselves ship in release 0.2 (PROMETHEVS_0.2.zip, see engine-0.2/INSTALL.md).
Copyright (c) 2026 Ryan Flavell, MAGNVS Ltd. The report, figures, logs and text in this repository are licensed under the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International licence (CC BY 4.0): you may share and adapt them for any purpose, including commercially, provided you give appropriate credit to Ryan Flavell, MAGNVS Ltd, link to the licence and say what you changed. DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 is MIT, copyright DeepSeek. Credits for third-party work are in THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md.
The engine, scripts and tools of release 0.2 (PROMETHEVS_0.2.zip) are Copyright (c) 2026 Ryan Flavell, MAGNVS Ltd, licensed under the Apache License 2.0; every copy and derived work must keep the NOTICE file. Third-party parts of the bundle keep their own licences (engine-0.2/THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md).
If you use or build on this work, please cite:
Ryan Flavell. Compress-then-Correct Decoding: The Full DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 on a Five-Year-Old Gaming PC. PROMETHEVS Technical Report 1, version 0.1. MAGNVS Ltd, October 2026. doi:10.5281/zenodo.23577839. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23577839
GitHub's "Cite this repository" button gives the same entry from CITATION.cff.
We build on DeepSeek's model and draft head and on the ggml and llama.cpp libraries. Ryan Flavell conceived the method and the ideas it tests, set the direction and the quality bar, decided what was built and tested, and checked the results. The engine code, the test runs and the drafts of this report were built together with AI coding assistants working under his direction.

articles.title: Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash
articles.body:
Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash: Fast and cost-effective with longer clips
Today, we’re rolling out Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash, and making it generally available across the Gemini API and Gemini for business. Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash introduces native 15-second video creation, multi-turn conversational editing capabilities, and enhanced reference following. We have dropped the price 30% from Gemini Omni 1.1 making it available at $0.07 per second for 720p video.
Here’s an overview of what’s new:
Fast and cost-effective at scale
Beyond the lower price, the workflow keeps costs down: you can draft fast at 360p or 720p, fix a detail with a follow-up edit instead of re-generating the entire clip, and then upscale your best creations to 1080p or 4K.
Longer clips up to 15 seconds
You can now generate and edit videos natively up to 15 seconds long, up from 10 seconds with Omni 1.1. You can also specify duration in one-second increments from 3 to 15 seconds, giving you room to tell complete stories, create product explainers, or produce full social ad spots in a single generation.
Better reference adherence
You can guide generation combining character, product, or style images, short motion clips (up to three seconds), and audio cues — and Omni 1.2 Flash holds onto those details from start to finish. Faces, garments, packaging typography, and brand colors stay consistent across camera angles, making it easy to turn existing product photography or character sheets into virtual try-on clips, catalog spins, and branded video ads.
Combining one model photo with front-and-back product shots of three outfits, Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash generates a 15-second virtual try-on sequence across 360-degree turns and match cuts while keeping the model’s identity and each garment’s cut, drape, and back details consistent.
More consistent results
You can maintain stronger character, object, and scene consistency from the first to the last frame, with less visual drift or morphing across motion and camera transitions. Whether you’re interpolating between a first and last keyframe, or extending a clip to build a longer sequence, products, characters, props, and environments stay consistent from shot to shot.
Given the same static studio lighting exhibition poster and five-layer animation prompt, Gemini Omni 1.1 Flash does not match the reference image as closely as 1.2 does. Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash builds the poster sequentially layer by layer on the dusty-pink cyclorama rising the hexagonal plinth, assembling the ribbed glass, warm filament, faceted crystal, and coiled-cord letterforms for HALO, GLOW, and LUMEN, and locking every material, shadow, and typographic detail consistently through the final frame.
Easier editing in conversation
You can refine the same clip turn by turn — such as swapping a product or background, changing the lighting or weather, or switching the aspect ratio — instead of starting over from scratch. Multi-turn conversational editing works across full 15-second clips, making it easy to produce ad variants for different audiences and placements without re-briefing or re-generating.
Starting from one generated clip, multi-turn conversational prompts swap the background turn by turn — from a striped pavilion tent to an oak forest, a stable with a white horse, a market fair, and a stone castle — while keeping both characters’ performances, armor reflections, and camera framing intact.
More natural speech
You can generate scenes with more fluid, natural-sounding dialogue, clearer lip-sync, and distinct multi-speaker conditioning. This will show up whether you’re directing multi-character dialogue in Flow, creating video explainers in Gemini for business, or creating polished, pro videos with avatars, music and narration in Google Vids.
Conditioned on one conservatory scene image alongside four character, mouth, and one-second voice references, Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash routes each sampled voice to the right character with expressive lip-sync and natural comedic timing across a 15-second animated scene.
More controllable, cinematic look
You can direct complex, continuous camera movements like sweeping FPV flythroughs to dramatic zoom-outs and orbits with significantly fewer unwanted jump cuts, steadier scale, and a more polished, cinematic look.
Guided by two architectural reference photos, Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash directs one continuous FPV drone flight across the piazza, through the bronze doors, and up through the Pantheon’s coffered dome to the oculus with zero jump cuts.
Longer clips with smoother motion and tighter consistency
Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash generates clips up to 15 seconds long that hold references together better than before. You can scroll through to see characters, text, and camera moves stay consistent across longer shots, multiple turns and transitions with no cuts.
Real-world results, from creatives to global brands
Businesses, startups, and creatives are already using Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash in their workflows. And for the first time, Gemini Omni is now generally available, backed by Google Cloud’s enterprise-grade infrastructure and security. Provisioned Throughput is available, and outputs carry an imperceptible SynthID watermark.
Get started with Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash
While development is ongoing to further improve things like fast sports action, rapid script changes and complex physics, Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash is ideal for businesses, developers, and creators producing videos at scale. You can get started with Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash today as it rolls out across Google’s products and developer platforms:
- For developers using the Gemini API: Prototype in Google AI Studio, explore interactive starter apps, and check out the developer documentation and pricing.
- For businesses: Try it in the Google Cloud console, and build enterprise solutions with the API.
- For everyone using Google apps: Direct scenes and multi-turn edits in Flow, generate 15-second clips at no additional cost in Google Vids with a Google account or Google Workspace subscription, create 15-second videos in the Gemini app (rolling out to Google AI Ultra subscribers), and scale video campaigns in Google Ads.

articles.title: Blender's UI and Runtime: Much Faster Than GPUI
articles.body:
Blender's user interface, as a library you can use from Python, Rust, JavaScript (React, Svelte), C, C++ and Dear ImGui. People spent decades building and optimizing Blender's GUI. It's battery and memory efficient, and super duper fast. We decoupled it, to give everyone a chance to build their own products with it. It supports multiple languages and frameworks, so you won't miss a beat! Website and full documentation: bui.preetham.top · Chat: Discord This README is a small book. Read it front to back for the whole story, or jump to the chapter you need. Every chapter links to a longer guide in docs/ or on the website when there's more to say. BUI takes the user interface of Blender (its widget drawing, its interaction rules and its look) and turns it into a standalone UI library with a small C core. Your code builds the widget tree and handles callbacks. Layout, input, drawing and presenting all happen in fast native code, on the CPU or the GPU. At the heart of BUI is the kit: a small runtime written in C. The kit holds every widget in one tree, lays them out, handles the mouse and keyboard, and draws them the way Blender does. The drawing code is a C port of Blender's own widget code, and the interaction follows Blender's rules. On top of the kit sit bindings: thin layers that let Python, Rust, JavaScript, C++ and Dear ImGui talk to it. What BUI is not: - Not Blender. It contains the parts of Blender's UI code it needs and builds on its own. You don't need Blender installed, and you don't need to know Blender to use it. - Not a browser. The Rust and JavaScript sides use HTML and CSS as a UI language, but there's no browser engine, no webview and no network. - Not a re-imagining. The widget drawing is ported from Blender's interface_widgets.cc, and the Dear ImGui support runs the real Dear ImGui. Blender's interface is famous for how it feels. You press a number field and drag: the cursor vanishes, the value glides under your hand, and you never hit the edge of the screen. You type 2*pi into a field and it just works. You type "ad cu" into a menu and it finds "Add Cube". Millions of artists have these habits in their hands. That interface is also fast and frugal. It redraws only what changed, sleeps when nothing does, and starts in milliseconds. BUI exists so that any app, in any language, can have both: Blender's feel, and Blender's efficiency. - You have a tkinter app and wish it looked less like 1998. Run it on BUI, unchanged. - You're building a tool for artists who already know Blender. Give them the panels, sliders and shortcuts their hands expect. - You write Rust or React and want a native desktop UI without shipping a browser. - You use Dear ImGui and want it to look and feel like Blender, with one build flag. - You're curious how a UI toolkit works. The source is readable, and the concepts are explained in plain words. Before you ship something with BUI, read the known limitations: no accessibility support yet, no input methods, and it looks like Blender, not like your operating system. You can drive BUI many ways, and all of them share the same C runtime, so they all get the same widgets and interactions: Not sure which to pick? If you already have code, use the row that matches it. If you're starting fresh in Python, the Blender components are the friendliest. - Number fields you drag with a hidden, continuous cursor: Shift for precision, Ctrl to snap. - Math in number fields, with Blender's own expression evaluator: 2*pi, min(4, 3), round(1.7), x if c else y. - Ctrl+Wheel steps values, Ctrl+C / Ctrl+V copy values, Backspace resets. - Drag across checkboxes to set them all. - Press-drag-release menus, pie menus, and Blender's fuzzy menu search: "ad cu" finds "Add Cube", typos are forgiven, recent picks rank first. - Ctrl+Z / Ctrl+Shift+Z on every UI edit, and inside a text field while you type; Tab between fields. - Blender's float display precision, multi-field vertical drags, and panels that collapse with Blender's animation. - The HSV color wheel, color ramps, curves, trees, lists, text areas, canvases, a node editor and Blender's File Browser. - Blender's Dark and Light themes, switchable at run time. - tkinter: all 7,846 public names of tkinter and ttk. Nine real programs behave identically on the standard library and on BUI. - Qt syntax: widgets, layouts, signals, QPainter, menus and timers. - Components: 45 Blender widgets, editors and templates. - Dear ImGui: from blenderui import imgui, pyimgui-style. - One pip install, no Qt or Tk widgets drawing anything. - All 113 HTML elements, drawn like a browser draws them; styled gives any subtree Blender's look, and Blender components (, {/* a Blender component */} ) } render(, { title: "Counter", width: 360, height: 200, gpu: true })bun app.jsx # run it (Bun reads JSX directly) npx bui build app.jsx # or ship it: app.exe, one 7 MB file Without React, @blender-ui/native gives you a DOM-like API: const { App, signal } = require("@blender-ui/native") const app = new App({ gpu: true }) const win = app.window({ title: "Hello", width: 360, height: 200 }) win.body.className = "m-0 p-6 flex flex-col gap-3 bg-[#2b2b2b] text-[#e6e6e6]" const clicks = signal(0) const label = win.createElement("span") label.textContent = clicks // follows the signal const button = win.createElement("button") button.textContent = "Add one" button.addEventListener("click", () => clicks.value++) win.body.appendChild(label) win.body.appendChild(button) These snippets are small. This is a larger example, a task list in React, and not the output of the code above: A task list in React (examples/site/js/todo_react.js); the DOM-like version draws the same Node.js 18+ or Bun. Prebuilt for Windows x64; on Linux, build the addon from source (npm run build in bindings/node) and windows are native. Guide: docs/javascript.md. The real Dear ImGui 1.93 runs on BUI: BUI's windows, input, CPU/GPU renderer, Blender's theme and the Inter font. Existing ImGui code compiles unchanged. C++: #include "imgui.h" #include "imgui_impl_bui.h" // see examples/imgui_demo.cpp static void frame(void*) { ImGui::ShowDemoWindow(); ImGui::Begin("Hello"); static float v = 0.5f; ImGui::SliderFloat("Value", &v, 0.0f, 1.0f); ImGui::End(); } int main() { ImGui::CreateContext(); ImGui_ImplBUI_App* app = ImGui_ImplBUI_CreateApp("Demo", 1280, 800, frame, nullptr); ImGui_ImplBUI_RunApp(app); ImGui_ImplBUI_DestroyApp(app); ImGui::DestroyContext(); } Python: import blenderui.imgui as imgui # C: cimgui.h · Rust: the blenderui-imgui crate state = {"value": 0.5} def frame(): imgui.show_demo_window() imgui.begin("Hello") _, state["value"] = imgui.slider_float("Value", state["value"], 0.0, 1.0) imgui.end() imgui.run(frame, title="Hello", size=(1280, 800)) C (cimgui.h, cimgui conventions: ImGui_Button, ImGui_ButtonEx, and the backend in cimgui_impl_bui.h) and Rust (blenderui-imgui) work the same way: use blenderui_imgui as imgui; fn main() { let mut value = 0.5f32; imgui::run("Hello", [1280, 800], move || { imgui::show_demo_window(); imgui::begin("Hello"); imgui::slider_float("Value", &mut value, 0.0, 1.0); imgui::end(); }); } Build with -DBUI_IMGUI_BLENDER_WIDGETS=ON (or the Rust feature blender-widgets) and ImGui's widgets become Blender's own: DragFloat is Blender's drag-to-scrub number field (Shift for precision, Ctrl to snap), SliderFloat Blender's number slider, checkboxes drag-toggle, menus and combos get Blender's menus. The rest of the ImGui API is unchanged. (The PyPI wheel is built without it, so from Python you get ImGui's own widgets in Blender's theme unless you build from source.) Dear ImGui's own demo with BUI_IMGUI_BLENDER_WIDGETS=ON: number fields, sliders, color rows and panel headers are Blender's A larger example, a scene inspector, once with ImGui's stock widgets and once with Blender's: The same ImGui code: ImGui's widgets (left) and the Blender-widgets build (right) (examples/site/imgui_inspector.cpp) Guide, coverage and the stock look: docs/imgui.md. The kit's API is one header, kit/include/BUI_kit.h, and it doubles as the reference: every function has a one-line comment. This is a shortened examples/kit_hello.c: a slider and a button in a native window. #include #include "BUI_kit.h" static void on_event(void *data, BKNode *node, int kind, void *ref, double a, double b) { if (kind == BK_EV_CLICK) printf("clicked %s\n", BK_get_str(node, "text")); else if (kind == BK_EV_CHANGE) printf("%s = %g\n", BK_get_str(node, "label"), BK_get_num(node, "value")); } int main(void) { BKNode *root = BK_node_new("frame"); /* everything is a node */ BK_set_num(root, "padding", 8); /* configured by property name */ BKNode *size = BK_node_new("slider"); BK_set_str(size, "label", "Size"); BK_set_num(size, "max", 10); BK_set_num(size, "value", 2.5); BK_node_add(root, size, -1); BK_geom_set_manager(size, BK_GEOM_PACK); /* Tk's packer, in C */ BK_geom_set(size, "fill", 1); BKNode *apply = BK_node_new("button"); BK_set_str(apply, "text", "Apply"); BK_node_add(root, apply, -1); BK_geom_set_manager(apply, BK_GEOM_PACK); BKContext *ctx = BK_context_new(root); /* input, focus, popups, undo */ BKHost host = {0}; host.emit = on_event; /* the window fills in the rest */ BK_context_set_host(ctx, &host); if (BK_window_supported()) { /* Win32, X11 or Cocoa */ BKWindow *win = BK_window_new(ctx, "BUI from C", 320, 120); BK_window_show(win); BK_window_run(); BK_window_free(win); } BK_context_free(ctx); BK_node_free(root); return 0; }cmake -S . -B build -DBUI_BUILD_EXAMPLES=ON cmake --build build --target bui_kit_hello The window below is a bigger program than the one above, a modifier stack: A bigger C program: a modifier stack (examples/site/kit_modifiers.c) Without a window system, render into a raster instead (BK_render(ctx, raster, w, h, full)), which is also how tests and screenshots work. Guide: docs/c-api.md. your code: tkinter Qt components Dear ImGui (C++/C/Python/Rust) Rust: rsx! / HTML / CSS / Tailwind / hooks JS / React │ │ │ │ │ │ └──── Python: options, signals │ ImGui core + BUI backend └── style cascade + taffy layout ◄────┘ │ │ │ C kit (kit/): node tree · geometry · input & interaction · Blender widget drawing · undo · animation · themes · Blender search/expr │ renderer: damage-driven software raster (parallel) or GPU (Direct3D 11 / OpenGL 3.3, instanced, opt-in) │ window: native Win32 / X11 / Cocoa window · stdlib Tk window · headless (tests, screenshots) - Your code, in any language above, creates widgets and says what happens when they change. - The kit keeps them in one tree, lays them out and handles input, following Blender's rules. - The renderer draws them, on the CPU by default or on the GPU if you ask. - Damage rendering keeps it cheap: a change redraws only the rectangle it touched, and an idle window uses no CPU at all. What's under the hood: - Blender's real UI code. Widget drawing is a C port of Blender's interface_widgets.cc (round_box_edges, widgetbase_draw, the shape tables), and interaction follows interface_handlers.cc. Color math, rects, text cursors, string search and expression evaluation are Blender's blenlib, copied in. A few interface files (string search, text-edit undo, float precision) are copied into kit/intern/blender/ and edited for the kit. The X11 and Cocoa hosts follow Blender's GHOST; the Win32 host is BUI's own. - One node tree. Every widget is one kit node. The C kit owns layout, hit testing, hover, focus, drags, menus, tooltips, undo and animation. - Damage rendering. A change marks only its widget's rectangle, and only changed tiles reach the screen. - Thin bindings. Python, Rust and JavaScript keep only what their syntax layer needs. More: ARCHITECTURE.md and How it works. These rules live in the C kit, so they work the same everywhere Blender widgets are drawn: the Python components, tkinter and Qt syntax, the Rust and JavaScript Blender components and form controls inside styled, ImGui's Blender-widgets build, and every C kit widget. - Drag to scrub. Press a number field and drag sideways. The cursor hides and wraps, so you never hit the screen edge, and comes back where the drag started. A float moves one click step per pixel; Shift moves at a tenth of the speed; Esc cancels and restores the value. - Ctrl snaps with Blender's rules: unbounded floats to whole units, angles to 10°, sliders to 0.1, 1 or 10 depending on their range, integers to multiples of 10. - Click to type, and type math: Blender's expression evaluator (expr_pylike_eval.cc) turns 2*pi, 90/4, min(4, 3) or x if c else y into numbers. This works in Blender number fields and sliders; plain text fields keep what you type as text. - Shortcuts on any value: Backspace resets to the default, - negates, Ctrl+Wheel steps, Ctrl+C / Ctrl+V copy and paste, right-click opens Copy, Paste and Reset. - Several fields at once. Drag down over a column of number fields to collect them, then sideways to change them together. Drag across checkboxes (or panel headers) to set them all in one stroke. - Panels collapse with Blender's animation; Ctrl+click opens one and closes the others; drag the grip to reorder. - Menus work press-drag-release or click; hover switches menu-bar menus; pie menus open around the pointer. - Menu search is Blender's string search: start typing in any open menu. It matches word initials ("ad cu" finds "Add Cube"), forgives typos, and ranks your recent picks first. - Undo everywhere. Ctrl+Z and Ctrl+Shift+Z work on every UI edit, and inside a text field while you type. A burst of typing or a multi-field drag is one step. - Float precision follows Blender: small values show the decimals they need. - Tooltips appear after Blender's half-second delay. Coming soon: typing values with units ("2 m"), Blender's search-as-you-type popups, and widget drag and drop. More: Blender's widgets. In Rust and JavaScript you pick the look per element: The components are Button, Checkbox, Radio, NumberField, NumberSlider, TextField, TextArea, ColorSwatch, Dropdown and ProgressBar. Each one is the HTML element it stands for, so every attribute, style and event works on it: rsx! {
// browser look // Chrome's slider // Blender's slider
// Blender's look inside
} div().child(Checkbox().checked(true)).child(Button().child("Apply")) // gpui syntaximport { render, NumberSlider, Button } from "@blender-ui/react" // , // DOM API: win.createElement("NumberSlider") cargo run --example forms: plain HTML, inside styled, and the Blender components The same markup, plain (left) and inside styled (right). Plain HTML looks the same in both themes. Blender components from Rust (site_components.rs) Python's Blender components (Panel, PieMenu, the node editor ...) are a separate, larger set. BUI has two renderers, and they draw the same pixels. - The software raster (gpu/intern/gpu_raster.c) is the default. It draws anti-aliased shapes with signed-distance coverage, like Blender's widget shaders, into one frame buffer, compares it with the last frame in 64×32 tiles, and reports only the tiles that changed. Big canvases draw in parallel bands on Windows (BUI_RASTER_THREADS). It needs nothing from your graphics card and uses the least memory. - The GPU renderer is opt-in: Direct3D 11 on Windows (gpu/intern/gpu_d3d11.c) and OpenGL 3.3 core on Linux (gpu/intern/gpu_gl.c). It's modeled on Blender's instanced widget drawing: each primitive is one 128-byte instance of a single uber-shader, so a frame is a few instanced draw calls. Text and images are cached in atlases. Frames render into a persistent target, so only damaged regions redraw; on Windows, a flip-model swap chain presents dirty rectangles. On Linux, libGL, libEGL and libX11 are loaded at run time (GLX for windows, EGL for offscreen), so no GL headers are needed, and BUI falls back to the CPU where OpenGL is missing. The shaders evaluate the software raster's formulas: the parity test finds 10 of 172,800 pixels that differ by more than 3/255, on both backends. Turn the GPU on: BUI_GPU=1 overrides the app-wide setting in code; BUI_GPU=0 turns the app-wide defaults off, but a window that asks for the GPU itself still gets it. Where no device can start, BUI quietly stays on the CPU (BUI_GPU_DEBUG=1 says why). Which one? A tool window, form or settings panel: the CPU (lightest on memory, idles at zero). A large or HiDPI window, lots of animation, thousands of items: the GPU (about half the CPU per frame, or less, for about 10 MB more RAM plus GPU memory). Servers and tests: the CPU. macOS: the CPU, for now (a GPU renderer there is coming soon). More: Rendering. Leave a BUI window open and walk away: it uses no CPU at all. Hover a button, and BUI redraws that button, not the window. - A change marks only its widget's rectangle as dirty (popups get a margin for their shadow). - Dirty rectangles merge (up to 24 per window). - If nothing is dirty, the loop doesn't render; it sleeps until the next input or timer. - Only the dirty regions are redrawn, clipped to their rectangles. - The raster compares the new pixels with the last frame in 64×32 tiles; a redraw that changed nothing reports nothing. - Only damaged tiles reach the screen (Win32 copies them, X11 sends each rectangle with XPutImage, Cocoa invalidates them, the GPU presents dirty rectangles). On the full component demo, that's about 0.7 ms for a complete frame and about 0.05 ms for a hover or number-scrub frame. Animations run only while something moves, paced to the display. More: Damage rendering. A window host puts a kit context in a top-level window and feeds it input. BUI_UI_SCALE=1.5 fixes the UI scale instead of following the display (1 is Blender's default, 20 px widgets). More: Window hosts. Your app's text looks the same on Windows, Linux and macOS, and it looks like Blender's: - Inter, Blender's UI font, is embedded (the variable version, with optical-size and weight axes). UI text is 11 pt at scale 1. - Rendered like Blender's BLF: BUI vendors FreeType 2.13.3 and renders with light hinting, Blender's gamma-1.43 coverage table, Inter's optical size, a real bold instance, no kerning (as in Blender), and Blender's text shadows. With BUI_TEXT_FREETYPE=OFF, stb_truetype rasterizes instead. - On the GPU, glyphs are drawn from their outlines with Slug by default, or from a per-glyph atlas like Blender's (BUI_SLUG=0, bui.set_slug(False), .slug(false), BUI_gpu_set_slug(0)). - Other fonts: BUI_FONT=path.ttf replaces Inter, BUI_FONT_DIR adds a folder to search first, blenderui::add_font (Rust) and BUI_text_add_font (C) register faces from memory, and CSS @font-face loads local files. - Windows' GDI text is opt-in (-DBUI_TEXT_GDI=ON, Rust feature gdi-text): ClearType-style hinting and system fonts, without Slug. Limits worth knowing: no per-glyph font fallback yet (missing characters show as boxes), no IME, right-to-left text is reordered but not shaped, no OpenType features. Font fallback and IME are coming soon. More: Text and fonts. BUI looks like Blender because it uses Blender's theme. It ships two: Blender's Dark theme (the default) and its Light preset. Both are generated by tools/gen_theme.py from Blender's own Blender_Dark.xml and Blender_Light.xml presets, over Blender 5.x's built-in defaults. Switch at run time, and every open window relayouts and redraws: Widgets, panels, the region background, the styled HTML sheet and ImGui's Blender style all follow the theme. Plain HTML keeps a browser's look either way. Inside each theme you can still color things yourself: bg / fg in tkinter, setStyleSheet in Qt syntax, color= on components, full CSS on HTML in Rust and JavaScript, ImGui's own style colors. BUI also includes Blender's icons: all 781 of Blender's SVG icons, rasterized with Blender's NanoSVG code so they're sharp at any scale. Use them by Blender's name: Button("Add", icon="ADD"), EnumRow(..., icons=[...]). Coming soon: loading any Blender theme file, beyond Dark and Light. More: Theming. pip install blenderui gives you four APIs in one package: - tkinter syntax (blenderui.tksyntax): every public tkinter and ttk name (7,846 of 7,846). Run existing programs with blenderui-tk app.py, or call blenderui.tksyntax.install() first. messagebox and simpledialog are Blender-styled, colorchooser is Blender's color picker, and filedialog is Blender's File Browser (BUI_FILEDIALOG=native for the OS dialogs). Look-only Tk options (relief, ttk.Style ...) are accepted, but the look comes from Blender's theme. Guide: docs/tkinter.md. - Qt syntax (blenderui.qtsyntax): widgets, layouts (box, grid, form, stacked), signals, QPainter, menus, timers and animations, QFileDialog as Blender's File Browser. Partial: model/view classes, docks, toolbars, splitters and Qt stylesheets are missing. Guide: docs/qt.md. - Blender components (blenderui.components): 45 components, from NumberSlider to NodeEditor. Reference: docs/components.md. - Dear ImGui (blenderui.imgui), pyimgui-style. Guide: docs/imgui.md. You can mix them in one process: windows, timers and the event loop are shared (bui.host). Every interaction runs in C, so tests can drive widgets headless. On the website: tkinter, Qt syntax, components, headless testing. The blenderui crate is a web-like framework drawn by BUI: every HTML element, CSS, Tailwind, HTML-like markup (rsx! / view!) or gpui-style builders, components and hooks. A taste: rsx! { // Tailwind as attributes, any variant, arbitrary values; typos fail to compile // control flow right in the markup
    {for item in items {
  • {item}
    • }}
{if dirty {

"Unsaved changes"

}} // real CSS, evaluated by the engine
}error: rsx!: `bg-sky-50O` is not a Tailwind utility; did you mean `bg-sky-500` or `bg-sky-50` or `bg-sky-100`? What's in the box: - Layout by taffy: block flow and wrapping text, flexbox and grid (every property, including grid-template-areas and named lines), tables, relative / absolute / fixed positioning (fixed boxes are placed against the window), scrolling, and bidirectional text. - CSS: selectors level 4, nesting, @layer / @media / @supports / @scope / @container / @font-face / @property, var() and env(), every math function, CSS Color 4 and 5. - Effects and animations: @keyframes animations and transitions (every longhand, cubic-bezier(), steps(), linear(), interruptible transitions), filter and backdrop-filter, mix-blend-mode, clip-path, masks, 2D transforms, border-image. Frames render only while something moves, and headless windows step a virtual clock (App::advance_clock). - Tailwind CSS v4, compiled on first use, with compile-time checks in rsx! and tw!. - Components and hooks in zopra, React or Leptos style, with optional props and keys. - Blender components, styled, and the theme. - Headless testing: Application::headless(), screenshots, simulated input. Not yet: async resources (use_resource), generic components, 3D transforms, OpenType features, multi-column layout. Guide: docs/rust.md, crate README: bindings/rust/blenderui, and the website's Rust section (including effects and animations). - @blender-ui/react: a React 19.3 renderer. HTML host components, CSS and Tailwind, events, Suspense, transitions, actions, and the Blender components. Hooks keep React's names but hold signals: pass one into JSX and a change updates that node without re-rendering. articles.title: Blender's UI and Runtime: Much Faster Than GPUI
articles.body:
Blender's user interface, as a library you can use from Python, Rust, JavaScript (React, Svelte), C, C++ and Dear ImGui. People spent decades building and optimizing Blender's GUI. It's battery and memory efficient, and super duper fast. We decoupled it, to give everyone a chance to build their own products with it. It supports multiple languages and frameworks, so you won't miss a beat! Website and full documentation: bui.preetham.top · Chat: Discord This README is a small book. Read it front to back for the whole story, or jump to the chapter you need. Every chapter links to a longer guide in docs/ or on the website when there's more to say. BUI takes the user interface of Blender (its widget drawing, its interaction rules and its look) and turns it into a standalone UI library with a small C core. Your code builds the widget tree and handles callbacks. Layout, input, drawing and presenting all happen in fast native code, on the CPU or the GPU. At the heart of BUI is the kit: a small runtime written in C. The kit holds every widget in one tree, lays them out, handles the mouse and keyboard, and draws them the way Blender does. The drawing code is a C port of Blender's own widget code, and the interaction follows Blender's rules. On top of the kit sit bindings: thin layers that let Python, Rust, JavaScript, C++ and Dear ImGui talk to it. What BUI is not: - Not Blender. It contains the parts of Blender's UI code it needs and builds on its own. You don't need Blender installed, and you don't need to know Blender to use it. - Not a browser. The Rust and JavaScript sides use HTML and CSS as a UI language, but there's no browser engine, no webview and no network. - Not a re-imagining. The widget drawing is ported from Blender's interface_widgets.cc, and the Dear ImGui support runs the real Dear ImGui. Blender's interface is famous for how it feels. You press a number field and drag: the cursor vanishes, the value glides under your hand, and you never hit the edge of the screen. You type 2*pi into a field and it just works. You type "ad cu" into a menu and it finds "Add Cube". Millions of artists have these habits in their hands. That interface is also fast and frugal. It redraws only what changed, sleeps when nothing does, and starts in milliseconds. BUI exists so that any app, in any language, can have both: Blender's feel, and Blender's efficiency. - You have a tkinter app and wish it looked less like 1998. Run it on BUI, unchanged. - You're building a tool for artists who already know Blender. Give them the panels, sliders and shortcuts their hands expect. - You write Rust or React and want a native desktop UI without shipping a browser. - You use Dear ImGui and want it to look and feel like Blender, with one build flag. - You're curious how a UI toolkit works. The source is readable, and the concepts are explained in plain words. Before you ship something with BUI, read the known limitations: no accessibility support yet, no input methods, and it looks like Blender, not like your operating system. You can drive BUI many ways, and all of them share the same C runtime, so they all get the same widgets and interactions: Not sure which to pick? If you already have code, use the row that matches it. If you're starting fresh in Python, the Blender components are the friendliest. - Number fields you drag with a hidden, continuous cursor: Shift for precision, Ctrl to snap. - Math in number fields, with Blender's own expression evaluator: 2*pi, min(4, 3), round(1.7), x if c else y. - Ctrl+Wheel steps values, Ctrl+C / Ctrl+V copy values, Backspace resets. - Drag across checkboxes to set them all. - Press-drag-release menus, pie menus, and Blender's fuzzy menu search: "ad cu" finds "Add Cube", typos are forgiven, recent picks rank first. - Ctrl+Z / Ctrl+Shift+Z on every UI edit, and inside a text field while you type; Tab between fields. - Blender's float display precision, multi-field vertical drags, and panels that collapse with Blender's animation. - The HSV color wheel, color ramps, curves, trees, lists, text areas, canvases, a node editor and Blender's File Browser. - Blender's Dark and Light themes, switchable at run time. - tkinter: all 7,846 public names of tkinter and ttk. Nine real programs behave identically on the standard library and on BUI. - Qt syntax: widgets, layouts, signals, QPainter, menus and timers. - Components: 45 Blender widgets, editors and templates. - Dear ImGui: from blenderui import imgui, pyimgui-style. - One pip install, no Qt or Tk widgets drawing anything. - All 113 HTML elements, drawn like a browser draws them; styled gives any subtree Blender's look, and Blender components (, {/* a Blender component */} ) } render(, { title: "Counter", width: 360, height: 200, gpu: true })bun app.jsx # run it (Bun reads JSX directly) npx bui build app.jsx # or ship it: app.exe, one 7 MB file Without React, @blender-ui/native gives you a DOM-like API: const { App, signal } = require("@blender-ui/native") const app = new App({ gpu: true }) const win = app.window({ title: "Hello", width: 360, height: 200 }) win.body.className = "m-0 p-6 flex flex-col gap-3 bg-[#2b2b2b] text-[#e6e6e6]" const clicks = signal(0) const label = win.createElement("span") label.textContent = clicks // follows the signal const button = win.createElement("button") button.textContent = "Add one" button.addEventListener("click", () => clicks.value++) win.body.appendChild(label) win.body.appendChild(button) These snippets are small. Guide: docs/c-api.md. your code: tkinter Qt components Dear ImGui (C++/C/Python/Rust) Rust: rsx! / HTML / CSS / Tailwind / hooks JS / React │ │ │ │ │ │ └──── Python: options, signals │ ImGui core + BUI backend └── style cascade + taffy layout ◄────┘ │ │ │ C kit (kit/): node tree · geometry · input & interaction · Blender widget drawing · undo · animation · themes · Blender search/expr │ renderer: damage-driven software raster (parallel) or GPU (Direct3D 11 / OpenGL 3.3, instanced, opt-in) │ window: native Win32 / X11 / Cocoa window · stdlib Tk window · headless (tests, screenshots) - Your code, in any language above, creates widgets and says what happens when they change. - The kit keeps them in one tree, lays them out and handles input, following Blender's rules. - The renderer draws them, on the CPU by default or on the GPU if you ask. - Damage rendering keeps it cheap: a change redraws only the rectangle it touched, and an idle window uses no CPU at all. What's under the hood: - Blender's real UI code. Widget drawing is a C port of Blender's interface_widgets.cc (round_box_edges, widgetbase_draw, the shape tables), and interaction follows interface_handlers.cc. Color math, rects, text cursors, string search and expression evaluation are Blender's blenlib, copied in. A few interface files (string search, text-edit undo, float precision) are copied into kit/intern/blender/ and edited for the kit. The X11 and Cocoa hosts follow Blender's GHOST; the Win32 host is BUI's own. - One node tree. Every widget is one kit node. The C kit owns layout, hit testing, hover, focus, drags, menus, tooltips, undo and animation. - Damage rendering. A change marks only its widget's rectangle, and only changed tiles reach the screen. - Thin bindings. Python, Rust and JavaScript keep only what their syntax layer needs. More: ARCHITECTURE.md and How it works. These rules live in the C kit, so they work the same everywhere Blender widgets are drawn: the Python components, tkinter and Qt syntax, the Rust and JavaScript Blender components and form controls inside styled, ImGui's Blender-widgets build, and every C kit widget. - Drag to scrub. Press a number field and drag sideways. The cursor hides and wraps, so you never hit the screen edge, and comes back where the drag started. A float moves one click step per pixel; Shift moves at a tenth of the speed; Esc cancels and restores the value. - Ctrl snaps with Blender's rules: unbounded floats to whole units, angles to 10°, sliders to 0.1, 1 or 10 depending on their range, integers to multiples of 10. - Click to type, and type math: Blender's expression evaluator (expr_pylike_eval.cc) turns 2*pi, 90/4, min(4, 3) or x if c else y into numbers. This works in Blender number fields and sliders; plain text fields keep what you type as text. - Shortcuts on any value: Backspace resets to the default, - negates, Ctrl+Wheel steps, Ctrl+C / Ctrl+V copy and paste, right-click opens Copy, Paste and Reset. - Several fields at once. Drag down over a column of number fields to collect them, then sideways to change them together. Drag across checkboxes (or panel headers) to set them all in one stroke. - Panels collapse with Blender's animation; Ctrl+click opens one and closes the others; drag the grip to reorder. - Menus work press-drag-release or click; hover switches menu-bar menus; pie menus open around the pointer. - Menu search is Blender's string search: start typing in any open menu. It matches word initials ("ad cu" finds "Add Cube"), forgives typos, and ranks your recent picks first. - Undo everywhere. Ctrl+Z and Ctrl+Shift+Z work on every UI edit, and inside a text field while you type. A burst of typing or a multi-field drag is one step. - Float precision follows Blender: small values show the decimals they need. - Tooltips appear after Blender's half-second delay. Coming soon: typing values with units ("2 m"), Blender's search-as-you-type popups, and widget drag and drop. More: Blender's widgets. In Rust and JavaScript you pick the look per element: The components are Button, Checkbox, Radio, NumberField, NumberSlider, TextField, TextArea, ColorSwatch, Dropdown and ProgressBar. Each one is the HTML element it stands for, so every attribute, style and event works on it: rsx! {
// browser look // Chrome's slider // Blender's slider
// Blender's look inside
} div().child(Checkbox().checked(true)).child(Button().child("Apply")) // gpui syntaximport { render, NumberSlider, Button } from "@blender-ui/react" // , // DOM API: win.createElement("NumberSlider") cargo run --example forms: plain HTML, inside styled, and the Blender components The same markup, plain (left) and inside styled (right). Plain HTML looks the same in both themes. Blender components from Rust (site_components.rs) Python's Blender components (Panel, PieMenu, the node editor ...) are a separate, larger set. BUI has two renderers, and they draw the same pixels. - The software raster (gpu/intern/gpu_raster.c) is the default. It draws anti-aliased shapes with signed-distance coverage, like Blender's widget shaders, into one frame buffer, compares it with the last frame in 64×32 tiles, and reports only the tiles that changed. Big canvases draw in parallel bands on Windows (BUI_RASTER_THREADS). It needs nothing from your graphics card and uses the least memory. - The GPU renderer is opt-in: Direct3D 11 on Windows (gpu/intern/gpu_d3d11.c) and OpenGL 3.3 core on Linux (gpu/intern/gpu_gl.c). It's modeled on Blender's instanced widget drawing: each primitive is one 128-byte instance of a single uber-shader, so a frame is a few instanced draw calls. Text and images are cached in atlases. Frames render into a persistent target, so only damaged regions redraw; on Windows, a flip-model swap chain presents dirty rectangles. On Linux, libGL, libEGL and libX11 are loaded at run time (GLX for windows, EGL for offscreen), so no GL headers are needed, and BUI falls back to the CPU where OpenGL is missing. The shaders evaluate the software raster's formulas: the parity test finds 10 of 172,800 pixels that differ by more than 3/255, on both backends. Turn the GPU on: BUI_GPU=1 overrides the app-wide setting in code; BUI_GPU=0 turns the app-wide defaults off, but a window that asks for the GPU itself still gets it. Where no device can start, BUI quietly stays on the CPU (BUI_GPU_DEBUG=1 says why). Which one? A tool window, form or settings panel: the CPU (lightest on memory, idles at zero). A large or HiDPI window, lots of animation, thousands of items: the GPU (about half the CPU per frame, or less, for about 10 MB more RAM plus GPU memory). Servers and tests: the CPU. macOS: the CPU, for now (a GPU renderer there is coming soon). More: Rendering. Leave a BUI window open and walk away: it uses no CPU at all. Hover a button, and BUI redraws that button, not the window. - A change marks only its widget's rectangle as dirty (popups get a margin for their shadow). - Dirty rectangles merge (up to 24 per window). - If nothing is dirty, the loop doesn't render; it sleeps until the next input or timer. - Only the dirty regions are redrawn, clipped to their rectangles. - The raster compares the new pixels with the last frame in 64×32 tiles; a redraw that changed nothing reports nothing. - Only damaged tiles reach the screen (Win32 copies them, X11 sends each rectangle with XPutImage, Cocoa invalidates them, the GPU presents dirty rectangles). On the full component demo, that's about 0.7 ms for a complete frame and about 0.05 ms for a hover or number-scrub frame. Animations run only while something moves, paced to the display. More: Damage rendering. A window host puts a kit context in a top-level window and feeds it input. BUI_UI_SCALE=1.5 fixes the UI scale instead of following the display (1 is Blender's default, 20 px widgets). More: Window hosts. Your app's text looks the same on Windows, Linux and macOS, and it looks like Blender's: - Inter, Blender's UI font, is embedded (the variable version, with optical-size and weight axes). UI text is 11 pt at scale 1. - Rendered like Blender's BLF: BUI vendors FreeType 2.13.3 and renders with light hinting, Blender's gamma-1.43 coverage table, Inter's optical size, a real bold instance, no kerning (as in Blender), and Blender's text shadows. With BUI_TEXT_FREETYPE=OFF, stb_truetype rasterizes instead. - On the GPU, glyphs are drawn from their outlines with Slug by default, or from a per-glyph atlas like Blender's (BUI_SLUG=0, bui.set_slug(False), .slug(false), BUI_gpu_set_slug(0)). - Other fonts: BUI_FONT=path.ttf replaces Inter, BUI_FONT_DIR adds a folder to search first, blenderui::add_font (Rust) and BUI_text_add_font (C) register faces from memory, and CSS @font-face loads local files. - Windows' GDI text is opt-in (-DBUI_TEXT_GDI=ON, Rust feature gdi-text): ClearType-style hinting and system fonts, without Slug. Limits worth knowing: no per-glyph font fallback yet (missing characters show as boxes), no IME, right-to-left text is reordered but not shaped, no OpenType features. Font fallback and IME are coming soon. More: Text and fonts. BUI looks like Blender because it uses Blender's theme. It ships two: Blender's Dark theme (the default) and its Light preset. Both are generated by tools/gen_theme.py from Blender's own Blender_Dark.xml and Blender_Light.xml presets, over Blender 5.x's built-in defaults. Switch at run time, and every open window relayouts and redraws: Widgets, panels, the region background, the styled HTML sheet and ImGui's Blender style all follow the theme. Plain HTML keeps a browser's look either way. Inside each theme you can still color things yourself: bg / fg in tkinter, setStyleSheet in Qt syntax, color= on components, full CSS on HTML in Rust and JavaScript, ImGui's own style colors. BUI also includes Blender's icons: all 781 of Blender's SVG icons, rasterized with Blender's NanoSVG code so they're sharp at any scale. Use them by Blender's name: Button("Add", icon="ADD"), EnumRow(..., icons=[...]). Coming soon: loading any Blender theme file, beyond Dark and Light. More: Theming. pip install blenderui gives you four APIs in one package: - tkinter syntax (blenderui.tksyntax): every public tkinter and ttk name (7,846 of 7,846). Run existing programs with blenderui-tk app.py, or call blenderui.tksyntax.install() first. messagebox and simpledialog are Blender-styled, colorchooser is Blender's color picker, and filedialog is Blender's File Browser (BUI_FILEDIALOG=native for the OS dialogs). Look-only Tk options (relief, ttk.Style ...) are accepted, but the look comes from Blender's theme. Guide: docs/tkinter.md. - Qt syntax (blenderui.qtsyntax): widgets, layouts (box, grid, form, stacked), signals, QPainter, menus, timers and animations, QFileDialog as Blender's File Browser. Partial: model/view classes, docks, toolbars, splitters and Qt stylesheets are missing. Guide: docs/qt.md. - Blender components (blenderui.components): 45 components, from NumberSlider to NodeEditor. Reference: docs/components.md. - Dear ImGui (blenderui.imgui), pyimgui-style. Guide: docs/imgui.md. You can mix them in one process: windows, timers and the event loop are shared (bui.host). Every interaction runs in C, so tests can drive widgets headless. On the website: tkinter, Qt syntax, components, headless testing. The blenderui crate is a web-like framework drawn by BUI: every HTML element, CSS, Tailwind, HTML-like markup (rsx! / view!) or gpui-style builders, components and hooks. A taste: rsx! { // Tailwind as attributes, any variant, arbitrary values; typos fail to compile // control flow right in the markup
    {for item in items {
  • {item}
    • }}
{if dirty {

"Unsaved changes"

}} // real CSS, evaluated by the engine
}error: rsx!: `bg-sky-50O` is not a Tailwind utility; did you mean `bg-sky-500` or `bg-sky-50` or `bg-sky-100`? What's in the box: - Layout by taffy: block flow and wrapping text, flexbox and grid (every property, including grid-template-areas and named lines), tables, relative / absolute / fixed positioning (fixed boxes are placed against the window), scrolling, and bidirectional text. - CSS: selectors level 4, nesting, @layer / @media / @supports / @scope / @container / @font-face / @property, var() and env(), every math function, CSS Color 4 and 5. - Effects and animations: @keyframes animations and transitions (every longhand, cubic-bezier(), steps(), linear(), interruptible transitions), filter and backdrop-filter, mix-blend-mode, clip-path, masks, 2D transforms, border-image. Frames render only while something moves, and headless windows step a virtual clock (App::advance_clock). - Tailwind CSS v4, compiled on first use, with compile-time checks in rsx! and tw!. - Components and hooks in zopra, React or Leptos style, with optional props and keys. - Blender components, styled, and the theme. - Headless testing: Application::headless(), screenshots, simulated input. Not yet: async resources (use_resource), generic components, 3D transforms, OpenType features, multi-column layout. Guide: docs/rust.md, crate README: bindings/rust/blenderui, and the website's Rust section (including effects and animations). - @blender-ui/react: a React 19.3 renderer. HTML host components, CSS and Tailwind, events, Suspense, transitions, actions, and the Blender components. Hooks keep React's names but hold signals: pass one into JSX and a change updates that node without re-rendering. README: bindings/react. - @blender-ui/svelte: Svelte 5 components (runes, snippets, bindings, keyed blocks, context, scoped

articles.title: Cuban: Facebook knowingly runs AI deepfake scam ads; docs say $16B fraud revenue
articles.body:
Mark Cuban keeps getting emails about a $294 diabetes cure he has never sold.
"Every single week I get emails from little old men and ladies saying, 'Will my cure for diabetes work?' or 'I just ordered your cure for diabetes for $294,'" the 68-year-old billionaire investor said on an August episode of Pivot, the podcast hosted by Kara Swisher and Scott Galloway.
Must Read
- Jeff Bezos backs a platform that lets anyone invest in rental homes for as little as $100 — 6 ways to build wealth like a landlord without actually being one
- Dave Ramsey warns nearly 50% of Americans are making 1 big Social Security mistake. Here's what it is and 3 simple steps to fix it ASAP
- A single line on your car insurance policy could be inflating your premium by up to 30% — here's what to change
Those ads are deepfakes built with an AI copy of his face and voice, Cuban said, and Meta (NASDAQ:META) runs them anyway. "Facebook knows the little old ladies are getting ripped off," he said. He called the platform "the worst of the worst."
The ads Cuban says Meta waves through
Cuban said some of the ads even include a disclaimer admitting the person on screen is AI-generated and the clip is meant as entertainment. By the time anyone gets to it, he argued, the pitch has already worked. "And to Facebook, that's good enough," he said.
"The point is, that defines the culture of the organization," Cuban said. A company that lets scammers go after people's grandparents, he argued, has shown what it will tolerate at every level.
Cuban does run a drug company — he co-founded Cost Plus Drugs, an online pharmacy that sells low-cost generic medications.
What Meta's documents showed
On Nov. 6, 2025, Reuters reported on internal Meta documents showing the company expected roughly $16 billion, or about 10% of its 2024 revenue, to flow in from ads pushing scams and prohibited products. By Meta's own internal count, users across its apps were seeing some 15 billion "higher risk" ads a day — the ones with obvious markers of fraud. One late 2024 document put that category's value at about $7 billion a year.
In a May 2025 presentation, Meta's own safety staff estimated the company's platforms play a part in a third of the scams that succeed in the U.S. Before Meta bans an advertiser, its automated systems must peg the account as at least 95% likely to be running a scam, the documents say. Below that threshold, the suspected scammer simply pays more per ad and stays live.
Meta spokesman Andy Stone told Reuters the documents "present a selective view that distorts Meta's approach to fraud and scams," and called the company's 10% estimate "rough and overly-inclusive." Complaints from users about scam ads had fallen 58% over the prior 18 months, he said at the time, and the company pulled down more than 134 million scam ads in 2025. The same documents note the Securities and Exchange Commission is looking into Meta over advertising tied to financial fraud.

articles.title: Meta’s refurbished Quest 3S headset is nearly $100 off right now
articles.body:
If you’re curious about virtual reality, Meta’s Quest 3S is a good entry-level headset for dipping your toes in, especially now it’s on sale in refurbished condition for $255.99 directly from Meta’s eBay storefront through November 8th when you use coupon code SAVE20TECH. For comparison, the headset recently dropped to $300 in new condition as part of Amazon’s fall Prime Day event, and currently retails for $349.99.
Meta’s refurbished Quest 3S headset is nearly $100 off right now
We also found discounts on the Philips Hue Gradient Lightstrip and a USB-C hub that doubles as a miniature photo frame.
According to eBay, the certified refurbished headset is in “like-new” condition and has undergone professional inspection and cleaning by the manufacturer. More importantly, it comes with either original or new accessories — including a power adapter, a glasses spacer, wrist straps, etc. — alongside a two-year Allstate warranty.
The Quest 3S strikes a middle ground between the Quest 3 and Quest 2. Like the pricier Quest 3, it runs on the speedy Snapdragon XR2 Gen 2 chip and supports the same library of games. It also comes with the same cameras for full-color passthrough, letting you interact with the world around you while wearing the headset. It comes with Meta’s Touch Plus controllers, though you can also use your hands to navigate menus and interact with some apps. And because it’s a standalone headset, you don’t need a PC or console to play games.
However, its display resolution and optics quality are closer to the Quest 2’s, which, while good, means visuals are narrower and less sharp. Still, as we noted in our review, those trade-offs are easy to overlook given the price, especially if you’re new to VR.
Three more deals worth a look
- Philips Hue’s 80-inch Gradient Lightstrip is on sale for $83.16 ($115 off) when you buy it directly from Philips’ online storefront with code OUTLET58. The two-meter lightstrip can extend up to 10 meters and display multiple colors simultaneously, while delivering up to 1,800 lumens of brightness with customizable lighting effects. You can also control it via Alexa and Google Assistant, or using either Bluetooth or a Philips Hue Bridge.
- Anker’s new Desktop USB-C Hub is currently available from both Amazon and Anker (with code WSPDV2ONVYED) for $79.99 ($20 off), which is $5 shy of its lowest price to date. The 10-in-1 hub features a built-in screen that not only displays charging speeds, but also doubles as a digital photo frame and customizable timer. It also sports an HDMI port, a DisplayPort connection, four USB ports, an ethernet jack, and SD and microSD card slots, letting you connect multiple accessories and external displays.
- Speaking of gadgets with personality, Orico’s adorable PixCharge Plus is on sale at Amazon in several colors for $29.99 ($50 off), its best price to date. The small, 10,000mAh power bank has a customizable 16-by-16 pixel screen that displays animations, scrolling text, and pixel art using a companion app; it also supports up to 22.5W fast-charging and comes with a built-in USB-C cable that conveniently doubles as a strap.

articles.title: We know 15k websites are infected. how do we tell them?
articles.body:
We've identified 15,579 websites that are currently infected with malicious JavaScript and between them, we conservatively estimate that they receive more than 135 million visits every month.
We know they're infected, and we have the evidence to back that up, but there's a problem: how on Earth do we tell them all?
As our Threat Intelligence capabilities at Report URI have grown, identifying compromised websites has become increasingly efficient. Unfortunately, responsible disclosure hasn't kept pace, and we're now finding infections considerably faster than we could ever hope to notify the affected organisations.
I genuinely don't know how to solve this problem, so I'm asking for help.
What attacks we're finding
At the core of it, we're finding websites that are running JavaScript that they should absolutely not be running! For some examples of how nasty this can be:
- Credit card skimmers - often known as 'Magecart', they target payment pages and skim full card details to send them to the attacker.
- ClickFix attacks - designed to trick users into completing a "prove you're human" challenge and instead installing malware on their device.
- Device exploitation - loading malware to compromise specific versions of iOS and install spyware, like DarkSword or Coruna.
- Redirects - these can send the visitor anywhere, including fake login pages to phish details, device security 'warnings', scams, and much more.
All of these are bad scenarios for the innocent visitor, and attackers change their payloads depending on their objective.
How these sites are compromised
There are many ways an attacker can get malicious JS onto a site, but here are the main categories that we group the initial vectors into from what we're seeing:
- Direct compromise - typically a WordPress vulnerability or similar, the site's own JS files are modified to include the malicious JS.
- Supply chain - a third-party script file that a site loads is infected with malware, and is then loaded on to the site, exposing all visitors.
- XSS - good old traditional XSS, a vulnerability in the site itself that allows JS to be injected.
- DeadTag - a threat group we named recently, buying expired domains that sites still load JS from, reviving them, and serving malware.
Unfortunately, there are a lot of different ways that this can go wrong, as we're seeing.
The scale of the problem
Right now, we have 15,579 unique sites that are infected with one of the malicious JS attacks listed above. Those are the sites where there is no doubt in our mind, and the list of sites where we have some suspicion but haven't got to 100% confidence is thousands more. Take September as an example, because we haven't quite finished processing everything from October yet, and this is the tally for new sites that we identified as being infected:
These are the sites that, as of today, are still infected. We remove sites once they clear their own infection as we have no concern about trying to notify them, so there were more than this.
In terms of traffic volumes, it's quite surprising how quickly this adds up. None of the sites in the list are global leaders, but we do have a huge presence of regional leaders. For example, if we look at .fr, .es and .de sites, some of them are really highly ranked sites in those countries, but they barely crack the Top 1 Million globally. Being a top site in France still gets you quite a hefty amount of traffic it turns out. Using various sources of data, and being ultra-conservative with our estimates, our list of currently infected sites is comfortably receiving a combined 135 million visits a month. That's a lot of exposure.
So, what do we do?
We continue to reach out directly to those sites that we identify as particularly high impact and try to notify them, though this is happening on an admittedly small scale. The process of responsible disclosure consumes a lot of resources, use of security.txt is low, and the vast majority of our emails and messages go unanswered. It's simply not possible for us to scale this up.
As these are sites we're crawling and identifying ourselves, we have no contact information like we would for a customer. So, as things currently stand, that's where we are, and I'd like to hear suggestions on what we can do.
If you're from an NCSC/CERT, especially in Europe where we seem to be finding a lot of impacted sites, please reach out to intel@report-uri.com and we'd be happy to provide a list of infected sites in your region. Hopefully you would be able to have more success in notifying the impacted sites than we would. 
If you're an organisation and believe having commercial access to our threat intelligence feeds would help you protect your own customers, you can also reach out to intel@report-uri.com for details.
Back to the original problem, though, and it pains me to say it but I don't have a clear idea on how we can try to have more of a positive impact. If you think there's something you can help with, an idea you'd like to put forward, or a suggestion on what we can do with all of this data, please drop by the comments below and I'd be happy to hear from you.
We have intelligence that could help protect millions of website visits, and we need help to turn it into action.

If you're from an NCSC/CERT, especially in Europe where we seem to be finding a lot of impacted sites, please reach out to intel@report-uri.com and we'd be happy to provide a list of infected sites in your region. Hopefully you would be able to have more success in notifying the impacted sites than we would. 
If you're an organisation and believe having commercial access to our threat intelligence feeds would help you protect your own customers, you can also reach out to intel@report-uri.com for details.
Back to the original problem, though, and it pains me to say it but I don't have a clear idea on how we can try to have more of a positive impact. If you think there's something you can help with, an idea you'd like to put forward, or a suggestion on what we can do with all of this data, please drop by the comments below and I'd be happy to hear from you.
We have intelligence that could help protect millions of website visits, and we need help to turn it into action.

articles.title: Pwn.college
articles.body:
You have entered the pwn.college DOJO, an education platform for learners to develop and practice core cybersecurity skills in a hands-on fashion.
Entering, you receive your "white belt" , signifying the beginning of your hacker life.
From here, you will learn cybersecurity by diving deep into the core of computing, using that journey to absorb cybersecurity concepts.
This will involve melding your mind to your terminal, whispering instructions to the CPU, and strumming bits directly onto networks.
That terminal cursor blinking above?
It will be your stalwart companion through this adventure as you practice, earn your belts , and, eventually, make perfect.
Every dojo has its sensei.
This platform is maintained by an awesome team of hackers at Arizona State University.
It powers much of ASU's cybersecurity curriculum, and is open, for free, to participation for interested people around the world!
The challenges created for pwn.college are, first and foremost, educational material, and are used to grade students at universities around the world.
Because of this, we would appreciate that you do not post writeups, walkthrough videos, and livestreams of challenge solutions to the internet.
Obviously, we can't enforce this, but we worked hard to make all of this public, and we would appreciate your help in keeping pwn.college a viable educational platform.
Please agree to these rules to continue to the material!
YOUR Journey — Next Steps 🫵
Whether you have just started, or have come far, there is always a next step to your journey.
The dojo or dojos listed below is that step, presented to you in the order that you should learn them.
Take a step, and the next will reveal itself.
Want to use pwn.college in your course? No problem!
You can use the videos and slides of pwn.college lectures freely for non-commercial purposes, but please provide attribution!
Additionally, if you use pwn.college in your own education program, we would appreciate it if you email us to let us know.
Evidence of wide-spread use of pwn.college for education will be a huge help for our various academic careers!
EDUCATORS: If you are an educational institution and are using pwn.college as part of a class, you can import our challenges (or add your own) into your own private dojo for your students! Create your dojo here.
CONFERENCES: If you are running a conference and would like pwn.college presence there (as a form of intense weekend-long training), please email us!
After pwn.college
Eventually, hackers continue their journey beyond pwn.college, becoming certain in their skills, achieving brown belt status (and able to, for example, usefully contribute to the cybersecurity industry and academia), before finally graduating to hacking masters: black belts.
But this, unfortunately, must happen outside of the dojo (for now!).
Some suggestions:
Capture The Flags (CTFs) are a great way to practice your hacking skills in a fun and ethical way. The most popular way to find upcoming events is at https://ctftime.org. There is also a list of introductory CTFs here. If you are at ASU, feel free to check out and join ASU’s enigmatic hacking club.
Wargames are another great way to practice your hacking skills. Whereas CTFs are short (normally 48 hour) events, wargames are not time-based. You can find a list of wargames at https://github.com/zardus/wargame-nexus.
There are many other awesome learning platforms, such as CryptoHack and OST2 that will help teach you explore new topics!
If you want to get involved with cybersecurity research, but don’t know how, consider joining us for an internship at ASU.
Contributing
The infrastructure powering pwn.college is open source, and we welcome pull requests and issues.
Some of the modules are closed-source, because they include source code and solution scripts, but others can be found on github.
If you are an educator, or otherwise someone we trust, and are interested in collaborating on the modules themselves, please email us at [email protected].
Likewise, drop us a line if you are interested in collaborating on the slides!
Resource Index
We use a lot of different resources and platforms.
Here they are!
