articles.title: How Remedy designed Control Resonant’s wildest mission: ‘Anything kind of goes’
articles.body:
Note: Some spoilers for Control Resonant’s “Recursions and Iterations” mission follow.
How Remedy designed Control Resonant’s wildest mission: ‘Anything kind of goes’
Time-travel stories are ‘illogical’ by nature. But for Resonant’s version to work, Remedy had to make the physical space a lot easier to follow.
How Remedy designed Control Resonant’s wildest mission: ‘Anything kind of goes’
Time-travel stories are ‘illogical’ by nature. But for Resonant’s version to work, Remedy had to make the physical space a lot easier to follow.
One of Control Resonant’s most memorable missions involves time travel — kind of. There are certainly multiple timelines intersecting, or maybe overlapping, or maybe running in parallel. As protagonist Dylan Faden, you meet some of the researchers who are trapped in and investigating these timeline anomalies. Dylan’s first encounter with the researchers is somehow not the researchers’ first time meeting Dylan. But before we can learn much more, time glitches out, and they all turn up dead.
That seems to be the end result in every timeline Dylan comes across, even toward the end of the mission. What does it all mean for this timeline, the one we’re playing? Did the act of tracking down the researchers change our timeline? Are we in a different timeline entirely?
I wasn’t sure what to make of it when I finished the mission, and I’m not alone — even the developers at Remedy had trouble keeping track of it all. “I don’t actually remember where we landed on with the writing,” says lead level designer Anne-Marie Grönroos, turning the question over to senior level designer Admir Burnic. “Like, are the researchers even there after the mission is done? Are they still living their life?”
Burnic isn’t sure, and I tell them I’m not entirely sure, either. But that’s not really the point of the mission. Like many of Remedy’s best sequences, the “Recursions and Iterations” mission is more about the unease of knowing something is wrong but not exactly what it is, the subtle horror of realizing generally what’s been happening but not necessarily why. Maybe the narrative team did establish a canon ending for the researchers and all three of us just missed it, or maybe it was ambiguous on purpose.
“It’s funny, when you’re dealing with this sort of time-travel stuff, timelines, whatever, there’s always this aspect to it where it’s almost illogical,” Burnic says. “So anything kind of goes. I mean, it could be intentional. It could also not be intentional.”
Prepare for (being inspired by) Titanfall.
Toward the end of “Recursions and Iterations,” there’s a mind-bending combat sequence in which a bunch of Dylans, presumably from the other timelines, glitch in to join the fight. Burnic says this was a somewhat late addition inspired by “Effect and Cause,” a mission from Titanfall 2.
There’s this time-travel mission in Titanfall 2. I was really inspired by that. I wanted to do something along those lines, but I was looking for “What’s the Remedy version of it?” And at some point I had this idea of glitches of Dylan showing up executing enemies. I remember it was fairly late in production, so it was a bit risky. I knew I can’t just go and pitch this. I have other stuff to do at the same time. So I was finding something that was relatively easy to do, a way to reuse Dylan’s animations that we already have. So I remember just going to one of our animators and going, “Hey, can you just throw me some of these animations? I have an idea.”
Either way, the storyline was a consistent standout for Remedy’s playtesters, Grönroos and Burnic tell me. What they had to fine-tune — and very intentionally so — was the language and narrative of the physical space. In the final version of the mission, Dylan has to travel between three different research stations in the labyrinthine Underpass, an expanse of floating concrete islands, to search for the researchers. Ambiguity here was going to be a problem.
“In the beginning, it was, like, identical stations, and we would more rely on the narrative content inside of stations to [tell you] what happened there,” Burnic says. In the final version, the stations share the same layout but are in visibly different states of disarray and disrepair. “We found a sort of language we could use. Station A was, ‘They were here for two weeks,’ station B [was], ‘They were here for three months,’ and I think the last one was the extreme one, which was like, ‘Oh, this was 10 years into this.’”
The team used that concept as a guide to visually differentiate each station from the others. “And that came very much from a need,” Grönroos explains. “When we had people playtesting that mission before, they didn’t even know how many stations there were. Like, there were people who thought there’s one station, maybe there’s six stations, who knows, because they look so identical and the environment is not that easy to tell apart, either.”
There were, aptly, a lot of iterations of this, and art was just part of it. One of the biggest changes was mechanical: You need the Reach ability, which allows Dylan to essentially grapple over long distances, to access the Underpass area to begin with. This wasn’t an explicit requirement early on, but it makes the floating islands of the Underpass much easier to navigate. And “it was the navigation issues that were keeping this mission down” during development, Grönroos says.
But Dylan’s abilities presented their own problems. “If I remember correctly, we wanted to have certain beats, certain narrative moments, being represented to you first, and I think one of the biggest difficulties for me especially was that Dylan as a character is so powerful. The gaps he can close with his powers is quite insane, right? And it was so easy to break [the flow],” Burnic says.
“I remember at some point kind of realizing that, however you twist and turn it, you can never really guarantee that a player sees this, and trying to guarantee it will be a bad design because it will be too hand-holdy,” he adds. “It was more like these narrative moments were pieces of the puzzle, almost. So it doesn’t matter which one you get to first, but hopefully the player will be able to put them together once they have all the pieces.”
With a supremely powerful character like Dylan, Burnic says, “you need to lean into it and just design in a way where you can trust the player.” And with multiple timelines involved, seeing certain things out of the intended order wasn’t going to break the overall story of the mission.
I certainly got turned around a few times in the Underpass and doubled back to look for collectibles I might’ve missed. But I didn’t struggle too much, and I understood the story Remedy was trying to tell — maybe not every single detail possible, but the most important beats, and definitely the unsettling, otherworldly mood it created.
That was ultimately the “fragile balance” they had to strike, Grönroos says: trying “to have enough guidance that you understand what you are doing and where you’re supposed to be going” without holding the player’s hand.
“It’s in the DNA of the whole game, really.”

articles.title: Tesla and SpaceX lose over $420B in combined market cap in the two days
articles.body:
The midterm elections have dealt a major blow to Donald Trump and his Republican Party, as well as to one of his biggest backers, entrepreneur Elon Musk. The two major companies controlled by Musk—Tesla and SpaceX—have suffered a sharp stock market correction following the Democrats' unexpected victory in Texas and their majority in the U.S. Congress.
Tesla shares fell 3.3% on Wednesday, and on Thursday the decline accelerated, dropping another 10.77%. SpaceX shares fell 3.8% on the first day and another 9% on Thursday. In total, the market value loss for the two companies is approaching $469 billion, or about €417 billion at the current exchange rate. On Wednesday, the depreciation amounted to €110 billion.
Given that Elon Musk controls 35% of SpaceX and 11% of Tesla, the loss in value of his personal wealth is around $189 billion (€170 billion).
Markets have interpreted the election results as an increase in regulatory risks for the business empire of the South African tycoon, one of the main funders of the Republican Party in the midterm campaign .
Musk's business empire has benefited in recent years from a very lax tax regime in Texas, along with regulations highly favorable to the development of data centers for processing artificial intelligence algorithms, one of his major investments. He has also capitalized on SpaceX's consolidation as the primary supplier to the aerospace agency, NASA.
Analysts consulted by Bloomberg believe that a Democratic-controlled Congress could strengthen oversight of key sectors for Musk, such as AI, and complicate a potential integration between Tesla and SpaceX.
The market reaction has been furious, especially since both companies are headquartered in Texas , a state Musk has made the center of his operations. The entrepreneur moved his residence there in 2020 and relocated Tesla's headquarters the following year, after his clashes with California authorities during the pandemic. He also established his large Tesla car factory near Austin, his largest production facility in the United States.
“Texas becoming a Democratic state creates a new political challenge for Musk, especially considering how much money he has invested in making it the center of his business empire,” notes Ivan Feinseth, chief investment officer at Tigress Financial Partners.
The Democratic victory in Texas also has a symbolic dimension for the entrepreneur. The new governor, Gina Hinojosa , advocated during the campaign for greater control over data centers, essential infrastructure for the development of AI-related projects. The outcome of the Senate elections in the state has also been interpreted by some analysts as a sign of rejection of Musk's growing political influence.
The billionaire has strengthened his political involvement with Donald Trump and the Republican Party in recent years, having donated nearly $450 million to Republican candidates , of which some $205 million went to campaigns in Texas. According to various estimates, he has donated more money in these months than investor George Soros spent on the Democratic Party throughout his lifetime. Furthermore, Musk used his social network X (formerly Twitter) to openly urge people to vote against the Democrats during the election campaign.
After the results were announced, Musk reacted ironically on the same platform. “Guess my space lasers for interfering with the election didn’t work this time,” he wrote. In another message, he stated that “ data centers in space are starting to look pretty appealing.”
The new political landscape could have implications for some of their companies' strategic projects, such as the potential merger between Tesla and SpaceX . Several analysts believe that Democratic control of Congress could increase political and regulatory scrutiny of this deal.
Despite the decline in the value of Musk's companies, other electric vehicle manufacturers reacted in the opposite way. Rivian and Lucid saw their stock prices rise amid expectations that a Democratic majority will push for measures favorable to the energy transition.
One of the most common interpretations among fund investors is that Elon Musk has capitalized on the wave of deregulation championed by Donald Trump in recent years. In the early stages of Trump's presidency, the entrepreneur even served as an external advisor to the administration, heading the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE), to try to cut public spending, much like Javier Milei's chainsaw campaign in Argentina. Ultimately, a disagreement between the president and Musk led to his temporary departure from the White House.
Beyond the midterm election results , doubts persist about the viability and timeline of several projects that underpin the high valuations of Musk's companies. The potential merger between Tesla and SpaceX remains in a preliminary stage, while initiatives such as robotaxis , humanoid robots, and Mars colonization plans continue to fall short of generating significant revenue.

articles.title: The New York Times is in talks to buy Letterboxd for around $330 million
articles.body:
The New York Times Company is in talks”exclusive negotations” to acquire Letterboxd, the social network for film lovers, for around $330 million, The New York Times reports. The Times Company, Sony Pictures Entertainment, and A24 were all recently rumored to be among those interested in buying Letterboxd.
The New York Times is in talks to buy Letterboxd for around $330 million
Rumors have been swirling about the film lover’s social network for a while, but the NYT reports it’s the buyer.
The negotiations with the Times Company have included the potential for Letterboxd’s co-founders to stay in charge but report to a Times Company executive. Letterboxd would likely remain standalone for the “foreseeable future,” according to the NYT. The company would also integrate the Times Company’s ad tech.
NYT spokesperson Charlie Stadtlander declined to comment. Letterboxd and current parent company Tiny Ltd. didn’t immediately reply to a request for comment from The Verge.
If the NYT does acquire Letterboxd, it would follow other major purchases like Wordle (in a deal in “the low seven figures”), Wirecutter (“slightly more than $30 million”), and The Athletic ($550 million).

articles.title: Replit rebuilt its sandbox engine with microVMs
articles.body:
Agent sandboxes are all the rage. A new sandbox startup is announced every couple of weeks. At Replit, we’ve been running sandboxes for nearly a decade. For years, we’ve run our custom sandbox infrastructure to make it easy for anyone to code online, and now Agents use these sandboxes to build applications without requiring any coding at all.
In the past few months, we finished rolling out a complete rewrite of our sandbox engine to improve security, capabilities, and portability across clouds. Our Bring Your Own Cloud offering brings Replit into customers’ AWS, Google Cloud, or Azure environments. As with most infrastructure work, we had to pull this off without anyone even noticing. We migrated hundreds of millions of projects smoothly, without data loss. In this post, we’ll dive into how we changed the isolation boundary, kept sandboxes fast, and made the new engine work at scale.
In this post, we’ll dive into how we changed the isolation boundary and kept our sandboxes fast. In Part 2, we cover how we orchestrate tens of thousands of microVMs at once on Kubernetes.
Why our work matters
Security, alignment, and containment are among the hottest topics in the AI industry. OpenAI’s Hugging Face incident and Anthropic’s evaluation incidents showed the world that autonomous agents can reach and harm real systems beyond their intended scope. Although these evaluations might have had reduced model safeguards, the clear takeaway is that traditional security boundaries are no longer sufficient in the age of AI. NIST’s agent standards initiative and congressional scrutiny put isolation, identity, and monitoring firmly on the industry’s agenda.
Sandboxing was not a new category for Replit. It was infrastructure our customers had depended on since the early days, and a foundation of our defense-in-depth approach. Early on, we realized that as AI agents become increasingly autonomous and widely adopted, the environment in which they operate needs to evolve too. The industry is now converging on the same requirements. DeepSeek’s DSec reinforces the case for elastic sandboxed compute infrastructure, and extra validation comes from open-source initiatives such as Kubernetes Agent Sandbox or Google’s AX and Agent Substrate. Early this year, selected agent-infrastructure startup rounds announced since 2025 totaled $59.3 million in funding across Daytona, E2B, Runloop, and Blaxel.
In November 2025, we set out to rebuild our sandbox infrastructure for more autonomous agents, persistent workspaces, and much higher concurrency. By February, we were already using it internally. We spent the following months hardening it and rolling it out.
The Path to MicroVMs
Our sandbox engine started out simple: stateless code execution in Docker, spread across Google Compute Engine VMs. Over the years, we added persistent workspaces, public endpoints, cached Nix packages, regional clusters, and bottomless storage with instant disk forks. As we set out to chart the path towards microVMs, we realized it would be much easier to start from scratch than to port the existing runtime from Docker to microVMs. This also allowed us to prototype and develop rapidly without risking the existing system.
A microVM is a lightweight virtual machine with its own Linux kernel and a minimal set of virtual devices. We use KVM to separate each sandbox from the host and from other customers’ workloads.
Containers still separate processes inside each sandbox. Hardware-assisted virtualization now separates the sandboxes themselves.
First, we needed to pick a virtual machine monitor (VMM) to run each microVM. We chose Cloud Hypervisor, which shares reusable rust-vmm components with Firecracker and includes features such as virtiofs, transparent huge pages, device hotplug, and live migration. Nested virtualization also lets us run development environments that launch VMs of their own. Hotplug and memory snapshots were particularly useful for our design, as they allowed attaching customers’ disks on demand to running warm-pooled VMs. We also patched Cloud Hypervisor to improve snapshot portability across our supported bare-metal and virtualized environments.
A minimal init process inside each microVM starts, stops, and monitors its containers. The host communicates with it over gRPC using vsock, a host-to-guest channel that does not require an IP network.
With all the primitives in place, we needed a single supervisor to set up the sandbox: start the microVM, configure its network, launch the containers, and run the servers clients use to interact with it through our river protocol.
These are general-purpose Linux VMs, not environments tied to a single app-building workflow. We use the same foundation for our self-driving company: agents investigate incidents, review code, analyze business data, and triage support tickets. In late January, we combined microVMs and remote filesystems with access policies, token proxies, audit logging, and our ZeroTrust network so teams could run agents in parallel against the systems they actually use. People set the goals. Isolated environments give the agents somewhere to do the work.
Security and isolation
Over the past year, there have been a large number of Linux kernel CVEs that can lead to Local Privilege Escalation (LPE): Copy Fail, Dirty Frag (xfrm-ESP), Dirty Frag (RxRPC), Fragnesia, DirtyClone, epoll race-condition PE bug, Bad Epoll, GhostLock, FUSE filesystem driver flaw. Many of these bugs have been around for years, but developments in AI have increased the rate at which these are being discovered.
Our previous runtime used Linux containers, which share the host kernel. A reachable vulnerability in that kernel can let an attacker escape a container and reach other workloads, credentials, or network endpoints on the host. Not every kernel CVE is exploitable in every configuration, but sharing the kernel makes a successful escape much more consequential.
With microVMs, compromising a sandbox’s guest kernel does not by itself compromise the host kernel. An attacker still has to cross the virtualization boundary.
Giving each sandbox its own kernel also lets us support tools such as Docker, which require privileges we could not safely expose in the shared-kernel runtime.
Minimized privileges and kernel surface
In our new design, a sandbox consists of a microVM with minimal runc containers running inside. Alongside the development environment, supporting services handle PostgreSQL, git backups, and secure request proxying. We considered a microVM for each component, but decided the extra overhead was not worth it and did not meaningfully change the tenant isolation model. Containers still provide separate namespaces, resource limits, and role-specific permissions inside the microVM guest.
The virtualization boundary does not make every process inside it equally trusted. We configure namespaces, seccomp, device access, and capabilities by role, so a user process does not inherit a monitoring agent’s permissions. Docker gets the additional privileges it needs inside the guest, and never reaches the physical host.
The VMM itself runs under an unprivileged identity with no Linux capabilities.
Smaller kernel, smaller attack surface
Our guest kernel starts from tinyconfig, not a standard distribution configuration. We leave out hardware subsystems a microVM does not need, including Bluetooth, wireless, USB, and display drivers. Your coding agent definitely doesn’t need a Nintendo Switch controller. Required drivers are built in, and guest initialization disables module loading. Given the increasing rate of kernel CVE disclosures this year, our minimal kernel build gives us peace of mind by entirely avoiding most of the affected code areas.
Daily automation keeps our kernel builds moving forward, with autonomous agents built on Replit handling the update workflow as part of our self-driving company.
We audited 6,211 Linux-CNA CVEs published from June 1 through November 4, 2026, using records from CVEProject and kernel.org. We avoided 5,969 of them (96.1%) by promptly incorporating upstream fixes or by excluding the affected code. 4,375 fixes (70.4%) landed even before disclosure, and 676 (10.9%) additional CVEs were excluded by configuration. At least 15 of these are explicitly described by the Linux CNA or Red Hat as enabling or potentially enabling LPE.
A recent example is CVE-2026-98432, the Linux TCP flaw Anthropic demonstrated could give a remote attacker root access. We incorporated the fixed kernel on October 12, before the CVE was published and more than two weeks before Anthropic described its exploit.
Never trusting the workload
eBPF programs observe process execution, file access, and network activity inside each sandbox. Linux Security Modules (LSM) provide hooks for enforcing restrictions at the kernel boundary. Together, these mechanisms give us detailed runtime visibility and a way to detect and block specific forbidden operations.
The system determining abuse and compromise is self-driving as well. Runtime telemetry feeds autonomous agents that continuously evolve our known detections and forbidden patterns. We will write more about how we automate threat research at Replit, but think of an always-on security camera that blocks harmful behavior immediately when recognized as such, and improves every time it discovers something new.
There is one security monitor for each sandbox, which operates on both the host and guest sides of the microVM. This component is supervised and is able to self-heal and restart after a crash or tampering, or when rolling out a new version. To guarantee always-on security, we optimized our continuous delivery pipeline so that the security component can be updated and hot-reloaded across all sandboxes running in production less than 15 minutes after changes are merged. Since we operate at the kernel level with eBPF and LSM, this also empowers us to move quickly with ad hoc remediations in response to zero-day kernel exploits even before a fix is available in mainline.
When eMudhra’s intermediate CA keys were compromised, certificate trust became an urgent security problem across the industry. Our sandbox harness automatically injected an updated CA bundle into all running sandboxes, letting us respond through an existing control path rather than asking customers to update each environment.
Isolate the network
Every sandbox can use the same private IP addresses because it has its own network namespace and routing table. Linux virtual routing and forwarding (VRF) keeps those overlapping networks separate, and connection tracking preserves the routing identity as traffic leaves and returns. Baseline firewall rules restrict access to cloud metadata and infrastructure address ranges, with explicit allowances where private connectivity is required.
For sandboxes with an egress policy, enforcement runs outside the guest. A host-side proxy checks TLS handshake hostnames without decrypting application payloads, filters DNS, and rejects traffic outside the permitted path. The guest cannot disable those host-side rules. Private endpoint tunnels similarly give the workload a local socket while keeping their credentials on the host.
Virtual-NIC rate limiters also enforce configured inbound and outbound bandwidth limits outside the guest, allowing bounded bursts while limiting sustained traffic. Changing the guest’s network configuration does not remove the VMM’s limiter. Bandwidth control contains resource abuse. It is separate from deciding which destinations are allowed.
Securing credentials and supply chain
Our managed connectors use credential brokers that forward requests to upstream services, such as GitHub and Google Docs. The broker attaches the upstream credential after performing authorization, so the workload can use the service without receiving its account API key. It removes caller-supplied authentication headers and strips sensitive response headers and trailers.
Package managers such as npm and pip also route their requests through a registry firewall. Any attempt to install known malicious dependencies and packages is blocked right away, preventing our users and their agents from getting harmful content into their sandboxes in the first place. Our coding agent is aware of this and autonomously takes care of replacing or removing blocked dependencies for our users to improve supply-chain security.
Bottomless storage
The filesystem of each sandbox lives on our remote block-storage service, which fetches data on demand. Starting a large workspace does not mean downloading its entire filesystem first.
To integrate with our custom block device service, we wrote a vhost-user virtio-blk backend. This process runs alongside Cloud Hypervisor and handles block I/O for the guest, making our remote disks appear as regular virtual block devices. It also moves away from managing hundreds of network block devices in one host kernel, which caused us lots of pain in the past due to unexpected deadlocks and node failures. This was also one of our first completely AI-written components back in the Claude Sonnet 4 era, going through five to seven iterations before consolidating to the current sync/async hybrid model running in production, which was what maximized throughput while keeping latency low.
Copy-on-write storage also makes forks cheap. A new disk can reference existing blocks and diverge as it writes. We also implemented graceful storage reconnection, so that rollouts can drain outstanding I/O, persist the disk, and reconnect without restarting the guest.
Keeping sandboxes fast
To spin up a sandbox, we need to boot a Linux kernel, pull images, start containers, and bring up guest agents. Our minimal guest kernel boots quickly, and warm pools let us do most of the remaining work ahead of time. Acquiring a sandbox takes roughly 500 ms, including attaching and mounting the customer’s volumes and configuring supporting services in parallel. That’s the handoff with disks mounted, as booting an empty VM takes much less.
Doing this for tens of thousands of sandboxes at once took a lot more than warm pools. In Part 2, we’ll cover how we orchestrate it all on Kubernetes.
What comes next
The system has been running healthy in production for a few months. We migrated hundreds of millions of projects without any disruption, and came out with faster boot time, stronger isolation, and evolved security primitives. We’ll keep investing in security and share more about the choices behind our Kubernetes orchestration and automated security research. In the meantime, go build something on Replit.
Acknowledgements
Authored by Connor Brewster, Jason Dellaluce, Adnan Abdulhussein, Luis Hector Chavez, and the rest of the Compute Platform team at Replit. If you want to work with us on cutting-edge infrastructure, our team is hiring.

articles.title: Brazilian Credit Guarantor Fund Data Breach Affecting PII and Payout Data
articles.body:
Comunicado importante
Atualização em 05/11/2026.
O FGC informa sobre um incidente de segurança envolvendo dados pessoais tratados pela entidade e esclarece o que foi identificado, as providências adotadas e os cuidados que recomendamos.
Identificamos acesso não autorizado a informações pessoais em ambientes relacionados aos processos internos do fluxo de pagamento de garantia do FGC. Até o momento, não foi identificada nenhuma evidência de que os dados tenham sido divulgados ou utilizados de forma indevida. Também não foi identificada nenhuma perda financeira decorrente do evento. A investigação prossegue, com apoio de empresas especializadas, para esclarecer a extensão do acesso e verificar se houve cópia, divulgação ou utilização indevida das informações.
A suspeita de incidente foi identificada em 26 de outubro de 2026. Desde então, foram adotadas restrições de acesso aos ambientes envolvidos, bloqueio de contas indevidas, preservação de evidências e revisão das permissões e dos controles de segurança.
A Agência Nacional de Proteção de Dados (ANPD) foi devidamente comunicada, em conformidade com a legislação vigente. A apuração continua, com apoio de especialistas, e as informações complementares pertinentes serão encaminhadas à Agência conforme o avanço das investigações. Os titulares afetados também foram comunicados.
Reunimos aqui as informações disponíveis e confirmadas nesta etapa. Caso a apuração identifique novos elementos relevantes relacionados a dados pessoais ou as medidas de proteção, atualizaremos as orientações pelos canais oficiais.
Quais dados foram afetados:
- Dados pessoais: nome, CPF, e-mail e data de nascimento;
- Dados relacionados ao pagamento da garantia: informações sobre os tributos retidos no pagamento e sobre o canal de distribuição pelo qual o investimento garantido foi realizado na instituição liquidada.
Principais cuidados e como se proteger
As informações envolvidas podem ser utilizadas para tornar contatos fraudulentos mais convincentes, inclusive em tentativas de uso indevido de identidade ou de obtenção de pagamentos e outras informações pessoais.
Por essa razão, enviamos comunicação aos titulares afetados e recomendamos atenção redobrada a mensagens, ligações e e-mails que mencionem informações pessoais ou relacionadas ao pagamento da garantia, especialmente quando realizadas por pessoas que se apresentem como representantes do FGC ou de outras instituições. Qualquer pessoa, ao receber algum contato suspeito, pode entrar em contato com o FGC.
Destacamos alguns cuidados importantes para a segurança de todos:
- Desconfie de contatos que solicitem pagamentos, senhas, códigos de autenticação ou instalação de aplicativos, mesmo quando mencionarem informações corretas sobre você;
- Não clique em links em mensagens suspeitas. Para acessar informações do processo de pagamento, use diretamente o aplicativo do FGC;
- Confirme informações relacionadas ao processo de pagamento de garantia pelos canais oficiais do FGC;
- Preserve as mensagens suspeitas e registre ocorrência perante as autoridades competentes se identificar tentativa de fraude. Neste caso, avise imediatamente o FGC.
Como os dados são protegidos e o que estamos fazendo
A segurança da informação é prioridade para o FGC que possui arquitetura robusta de proteção, além de equipes especializadas que atuam no monitoramento, na detecção e resposta a ameaças. Os ambientes utilizavam mecanismos de autenticação e controle de acesso. Após a identificação do incidente, restringimos os acessos aos ambientes envolvidos, desabilitamos contas indevidas, reforçamos o monitoramento e preservamos evidências para a investigação. A revisão de permissões e a validação dos controles de segurança permanecem em andamento.
O tema está sendo tratado com a máxima prioridade, tendo como principal preocupação o apoio aos titulares de dados afetados e a revisão contínua dos mecanismos de proteção de dados e de segurança da informação.
Atualizações e orientações sobre o incidente serão disponibilizadas nesta página: fgc.org.br/comunicado.
Para obter mais detalhes sobre dados pessoais ou esclarecer dúvidas específicas, entre em contato com nossa central de atendimento pelo e-mail: atendimento.credores@fgc.org.br.
 
Seguimos à disposição para prestar esclarecimentos e apoiar você nas medidas de prevenção.
Atenciosamente,
Fundo Garantidor de Créditos - FGC
Encarregado de dados – DPO
privacidade@fgc.org.br

articles.title: Pentagon offers battery startup 6K $250M loan to build U.S. factory
articles.body:
Batteries are everywhere, even on the battlefield, which helps explain the Pentagon’s recent interest in building more domestic manufacturing capacity.
The 12-year-old, North Andover, Massachusetts-based startup 6K announced Thursday that it won conditional approval for a $250 million loan from the Department of Defense to build a factory in Tennessee. The plant will use a unique microwave-powered process to produce battery materials that don’t rely on Chinese suppliers.
The company previously received a $50 million grant from the Department of Energy under the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law, though that 2023 grant was canceled by the Trump administration in a chaotic sweep of Biden-era awards, forcing 6K to reapply.
The factory was originally slated to open in 2024, but the grant cancelation and uncertainties in the EV market forced the company to rejigger its plans.
6K’s manufacturing process uses microwaves to heat metals into a plasma and then deposit them onto a surface, reducing the number of steps required to make cathode material, a key battery component. The company says the process can work on a number of different battery types, including lithium iron phosphate (LFP).

articles.title: As the Japanese Countryside Empties Out, Wildlife Is Disappearing
articles.body:
The Japanese population is in decline, but the downward trend is especially pronounced in rural areas. The loss of people might be expected to lead to a resurgence of wildlife. But paradoxically, where farms have been abandoned, wildlife is also disappearing.
Researchers say that small farms in the Japanese foothills have created mosaic landscapes with rice paddies, open pastures, and scattered woodlands that provide homes to many kinds of wildlife. Where humans cut down trees for firewood and gathered leaves for fertilizer, they made room for orchids and azaleas, Nature reports. Where farmers dug rice paddies, they made a home for rice fish and heike fireflies. Broadly speaking, many species found on farms have evolved together with humans, scientists say.
A 2025 study from Japan found that biodiversity was stable only in places where the human population was also stable. In areas where the population had declined, researchers recorded a drop in the abundance of butterflies, fireflies, frogs, birds, and native plants.
The trends in Japan mirror those in many other nations, from Spain to China, where rural areas are emptying out as people move to cities in search of work. Landscapes that were shaped by people are being taken back by nature, but often to the detriment of species that depended on human tending.
A recent study of the Lake Constance region in the European Alps found that plant diversity peaked in the medieval era, when small farms created a patchwork of fields, pastures, and forests that supported a greater array of plants than either the closed forests that came before or the industrial farms that would follow.
“The broader lesson is that, in modern conservation, the choice isn’t simply between farming and biodiversity,” said its lead author, Adam Spitzig, a PhD candidate at Stanford University. Small, diversified farms, he said, “can boost and sustain biodiversity while supporting food production.”

articles.title: Just about anyone can rent access to White House IP addresses
articles.body:
Someone at the White House appears to be running software that could enable outsiders to rent access on the presidential network for just “a few dollars,” as reported by Krebs on Security and The Register. That’s according to findings from the security firms Layer3 Intel and Synthient, which discovered residential proxy activity on the White House network.
Just about anyone can rent access to White House IP addresses
Security researchers discovered residential proxy activity on the White House’s network.
A residential proxy opens up a way for people to rent access to a home IP address and route their internet traffic through it, allowing them to conceal where their activity is actually coming from. Some apps and browser extensions include third-party software development kits (SDKs) that put proxy nodes on a user’s device — whether users know it or not. Third-party services can then sell access to the residential proxies on users’ devices.
As noted by the cybersecurity firm Spur, people can legitimately use residential proxies for purposes like ad verification and quality assurance testing, but bad actors can also use them to bypass geolocation controls and defensive filters. Hackers have used residential proxies for all kinds of malicious activity, including to create botnets and carry out account takeovers.
At the White House, Layer3 Intel found that 28 residential proxy services routed traffic out of the network from October 5th to November 3rd. It notes that this activity typically happens between 5PM ET and midnight. “That pattern suggests a person rather than a public guest Wi-Fi network: someone regularly on the White House network late into the evening, whose device is infected with a proxy SDK,” Layer3 says. The SDK in question might be linked to the watch party app Rave, according to Synthient, which says the app “bundles 12 proxy SDKs into the platform.”
Synthient found “a number of Windows 10 and Windows 11 devices on the White House’s network beaconing to known proxy providers like Geonode, Infatica and Mellowtel.” As noted by Krebs on Security, Infatica is a proxy service founded by Vladimir Fomenko, the owner of King Servers, which was linked to 2016 cyberattacks on election systems in Illinois and Arizona.
Layer3 warns that the residential proxy is “public access,” adding that “anybody can obtain it by signing up to a public residential proxy service, paying a few dollars and sending requests through it.”

articles.title: Chip stocks get slaughtered as Wall Street in worst post-midterm day since 1896
articles.body:
Wall Street's midterm celebration lasted one day. Chip stocks got taken to the woodshed Thursday, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average (^DJI) fell 3.4%, its worst second session after a midterm election in data going back to its start in 1896.
It took the Nasdaq Composite (^IXIC) six minutes to erase its entire post-election rally. Then the selling got worse.
The tech-heavy index closed down 5.5%, and the S&P 500 (^GSPC) lost 4.4%. It was the worst day for both since the April 2025 tariff crash.
Investors bought stocks Wednesday after Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress, helped by falling oil prices and lower Treasury yields. Thursday, the focus shifted to what a Democratic Congress could mean for the AI build-out, and in particular for the data centers driving it.
It was also the S&P 500's worst second day after a midterm in data going back nearly a century. The previous low came in 2002, when the index fell about 2.3%.
This week has an echo from 1896. The day after William McKinley won the White House that November, the Dow jumped about 4.5%, then gave back about 2% the next session. On Wednesday, the Dow jumped 3%, its best day after a midterm since 1982.
The Nasdaq-100 (^NDX), in correction territory since Monday, fell 6.4% for its worst day since March 2020. The broader Nasdaq Composite joined it, closing nearly 12% below its Oct. 6 record. Both indexes also closed below their 200-day moving averages for the first time since April. Many traders treat that line as the boundary between an uptrend and a downtrend.
The PHLX Semiconductor Index (^SOX) sank 12%, its worst day since March 2020, leaving it about 38% below its June record.
The S&P 500 shed about $3 trillion in market value. Nvidia (NVDA) alone lost about $450 billion, and chipmakers as a group gave up more than $1.5 trillion.
Memory and storage stocks took the worst of it, with SanDisk (SNDK), Western Digital (WDC), Seagate (STX), and Micron (MU) all suffering steep double-digit losses. AMD (AMD), Marvell (MRVL), Arm (ARM), and Lam Research (LRCX) fell sharply too. Even the biggest names, Nvidia, Broadcom (AVGO), and Taiwan Semiconductor (TSM), fell 9% or more.
The damage spread across the AI supply chain. Cloud provider Nebius (NBIS) fell double digits and CoreWeave (CRWV) nearly 10%, along with networking and optical names Astera Labs (ALAB), Lumentum (LITE), Coherent (COHR), Dell (DELL), Corning (GLW), and Quanta Services (PWR).
Speculative favorites went down with them. Tesla (TSLA), SpaceX (SPCX), Robinhood (HOOD), Coinbase (COIN), and Strategy (MSTR) each fell 9% or more. (Disclosure: Yahoo Finance has a partnership with Coinbase.)

articles.title: What Else Could It Mean? A Book Surveys the Playful, Iconoclastic Works of James Wines
articles.body:
What Else Could It Mean? A Book Surveys the Playful, Iconoclastic Works of James Wines
It’s not uncommon for artists and architects to espouse a desire for breaking conventions and pushing boundaries, but so few have embodied such a mandate as James Wines. An unparalleled devotee of wit and play, Wines is behind SITE (Sculpture in the Environment), a New York-based studio founded in 1970 with a portfolio that spans commercial construction, urban infrastructure, public art, and more. No matter the project, SITE’s approach is rooted in questioning the division between art and architecture and defying expectations.
In the preface to the new book, What Else Could It Mean?, Wines describes how he spent months in Rome after college soaking in the religious designs and civically unified architecture, which inspired what became his signature mode of working. When he returned to the U.S. to continue teaching at New York University, he asked his students to create with the opposite approach, one that tapped into a fractured and diverse contemporary landscape. “What else could it mean?” became a driving ethos that centered around “architecture as a critique of itself, as an inversion of design expectations, as humorous insights and the absorption of context as a motivating source of ideas,” he writes.
Published by Skira, What Else Could It Mean? showcases dozens of projects from the SITE oeuvre. The most iconic of the studio’s works are designs for BEST Products Company, a big box store that operated for four decades. Owners Sydney and Frances Lewis tapped Wines to create unconventional structures for their showrooms, which included a building that appeared to sink into the ground at an angle and another that split open as the base fractured from the rest of the facade.
The BEST designs are just a piece of SITE’s broader commentary on commercialization. There’s also “Ghost Parking Lot,” an enormous, immovable public art project in Hamden, Connecticut, that buried twenty cars beneath asphalt. Forever halted outside the shopping mall, the immobile vehicles became ghostly signals of endless consumption and urban sprawl.
What Else Could It Mean? collects Wines’ drawings, renderings, and writings across five decades, presenting these rarely seen documents alongside archival photos of realized projects. SITE’s ethos has particular relevancy today, especially as it challenges the inherent accessibility of art and architecture and advocates for a more democratic approach to collective life. Designer and curator Phillip Denny writes in the introduction:
These are works that engage their context, invite participation, and reward curiosity regardless of one’s background. It is art and architecture for the popular public that anyone can stop in front of, be surprised by, laugh at, and think about without a guidebook. Often ironic but never cynical, always generous and ecumenical, SITE created art where people least expected to find it, in the “junk-culture world of the commercial strip and suburban sprawl.”
Get your copy of What Else Could It Mean? on Bookshop, and explore more of SITE’s works on its website.

articles.title: Show HN: Agents infer Lego mechanisms from sources, then animate them
articles.body:
Give an LDraw LEGO© model to an AI agent, get back a Blender-animated version of it.
The agent will:
- Reverse-engineer (infer) the LDraw model's mechanics from its .mpd source code file 🤓
- Study the discovered mechanisms.
- Plan the interactions between their different mechanical components.
- And finally, turn those plans into python code for Blender, that will:
  - Create the required rigs for controlling the different mechanisms.
  - Animate them according to plan! 🤯
Note
The installation process will install every required tool and dependency locally on this project repo, in order to avoid polluting the host OS.
However, there is a requirement of setting several env vars on rc files, like e.g. .bashrc or .zshrc
The installed dependencies, like e.g. Blender, are git-ignored by default.
You'll need Python 3.12+ installed.
Start by cloning the repo and running the setup script, pick the right one for your OS:
git clone https://github.com/anteloc/ldraw-mecha.git
cd ldraw-mecha
./setup-macos.sh            # or ./setup-linux.sh, ./setup-win-wsl.sh
At the end of the setup process, you'll get a snippet with the env vars to be added to your shell profile (.bashrc, .zshrc, etc.), something like e.g.:
# >>> ldraw-mecha (from setup-macos.sh) >>>
export LDRAW_DIR="/Users/me/ldraw-mecha/data/ldraw"
export LDRAWDIR="$LDRAW_DIR"
export BLENDER_BIN="/Users/me/ldraw-mecha/bin/Blender.app/Contents/MacOS/Blender"
export LEOCAD="/Users/me/ldraw-mecha/bin/LeoCAD.app/Contents/MacOS/LeoCAD"
export LDRAW_XRAY_CACHE="/Users/me/ldraw-mecha/.cache/ldraw-xray"
export LDRAW_ANNOTATOR_DB="/Users/me/ldraw-mecha/data/ldraw-info.db"
# export TYPESAFE_API_KEY=...   # optional: Jev semantic search (jev-rerank)
# other env vars...
# <<< ldraw-mecha <<<
If you're on VS Code or a terminal, restart it in order to get an updated env with the newly added env vars.
For inspecting and selecting one pre-annotated model to animate, open the annotated models selector by running:
python3 model-selector/serve.py
Then, take a look at the Process guide for a step-by-step usage example.
Note
More samples available at: Gallery
Animations have been generated from original models, not from ai-generated ones.
These are some samples of animations by different agents, take a look at their Summaries for more details.
- Agent: Claude Sonnet 5.5
- Original model: 42043-1_Flatbed-Trailer.mpd
- Context: The model was too large and complex for fully animating it, finally I accepted Sonnet's suggestion about animating the crane alone.
Original
- Agent: Claude Sonnet 5.5
- Original model: 3625-1.mpd
- Context: Asked for an in-place animation, to avoid the plane moving around.
- Agent: Claude Opus 5.5
- Original model: None
- Context: This one is actually a generated composition, from several different minifigs, to be used as a "howto reference" for other agents also animating minifigs.
After publishing LDraw Nova, a sibling project for agentic generation of LDraw models, several people reached out to me asking about if models could be animated somehow.
During the development of Nova, I noticed that adding some special annotations to .mpd original model source files, and then giving those to agents, would:
- Help agents in understanding how to build other different models.
- But also, in understanding how a model was built.
Which gave me the idea that, maybe, an agent would also understand how a model would work.
As a first step to it, I gave annotated models to different agents, and prompted them to infer (reverse-engineer) their constituent submodels (see Haiku 5.5. experiment below).
Results from inference experiments were both pretty good and consistent across different agents, and I also noticed the following: many of the submodels inferred were actually mechanisms.
After questioning several agents about those inferred mechanisms, regarding how would they actually work, I also got consistent results: agents would describe behaviours based on the descriptions for the parts on a mechanism! 🤯
At this point, I had the following:
- Agents would split and refine models into submodels and mechanisms.
- Agents would understand each mechanism in isolation.
- Agents would understand how individual mechanisms worked.
The result of an actual divide-and-conquer process, right? 🤓
Which would make handling individual mechanisms manageable. 🤩
Now, there was the matter of giving agents the means to actually animate mechanisms they already knew how they worked.
I was playing with Blender MCP at the time, and Blender looked promising as a tool that would provide agents a way to manipulate LDraw models in 3D, imported into Blender as glTF (.glb) files.
But there was still an open issue:
How to map from a refined model source code an agent would understand, to its equivalent 3D model in glTF format an agent could manipulate?
And the solution I found was:
Annotate the 3D glTF model's nodes with the same annotations as the source code, so the agent would:
- Outside Blender: plan on submodels 🤔 and parts as source code.
- Inside Blender: execute on matching nodes ✨ on the 3D glTF model.
Now, I had a draft for a process, but no tools for the agent to use and carry it forward.
Given that the process would require a high amount of complex geometric and spatial calculations, I asked the agent to derive a new python toolset from the one created for ldraw-nova
The new python toolset I refined iteratively, by giving the agent simple models at the beginning, and increasingly complex ones each time.
And to test it, I gave an agent instructions to:
- first, plan from an annotated and refined .mpd model
- then, generate a glTF 3D version of it, with matching annotations
- then, upload it to Blender
- and then, produce the Blender python scripts that would animate the model as planned.
And it finally worked! 🚀🚀🚀
(but not perfectly) 😜

This is not an executable code fragment, but more like a 3D CAD model fragment written in LDraw language.

- the first 0-line following every 0 FILE line is the "description line" for the submodel, according to the LDaw standard
- add the description for every submodel there, a one-liner, as a person would describe it while looking at it
- at the answer, first place the parent model, then the child one(s) and then the grandchildren, and then descendants... etc.: go from containers or parents to containees or children, children of children. etc.
